title: From evading an abusive marriage to dying from a face lift, this is Nellie Melba
text:
Dame Nellie Melba was the Kylie Minogue of her time, an opera singer from Richmond, Melbourne, who became a global superstar in the early 20th century.

The prima donna is immortalised on our $100 note (if you've seen one of those around lately), yet she seems to have a lost a bit of currency and is now seen by some as a bit musty, fusty and boring.

But when we made an episode about her (or two, as it turns out) on ABC history podcast The Dead Can't Sue, we discovered that her life was filled with drama and tragedy worthy of the best operas.

It's no wonder a dessert, snack and an exit strategy all bear her name.

'Colonial gem'

Melba, whose real name was Helen Porter Mitchell, was born in 1861, the eldest of 10 surviving children. She played instruments and sang from an early age, under her mother's influence.

Her father was a building contractor whose fortunes were on the rise, but as a conservative presbyterian, he was opposed to music as a career for his daughter.

However, singing at church events or for charity was acceptable, so in 1869, eight-year-old Melba had her first public performance. The 700-strong audience demanded three encores from the kid.

Nellie Melba, her father, David Mitchell, and Nellie's niece, in Melbourne, 1903. (Supplied: Bain News Service)

Historian Leigh Boucher, co-host of The Dead Can't Sue, says: "She already had a reputation as this growing colonial gem."

At the same time, Melba was also a tomboy, which led her father to pack her off to a boarding school for young women.

"[This] was more of a finishing school rather than a robust, rounded education. She ended up getting booted out for misbehaviour," Boucher says.

Melba did end up with a well-rounded education, including in music, at Presbyterian Ladies College. Her cheekiness continued; in one instance she dressed up as a nun and solicited donations for a fake charity.

But Melba's joyful adolescence well and truly ended after her mother and a beloved sister died in 1880.

After that, her father moved the family to Mackay in Queensland to run a sugar mill, and Melba, being the eldest daughter, had to run the household.

Melba gets hitched and finally makes her debut

Happily, Mackay was not, as she might've assumed, an uncultured colonial outpost and Melba slotted right into the town's thriving amateur music scene.

The 21-year-old also met Charles Nesbitt Frederick Armstrong, a son of an Irish baronet who had been sent to the colonies for being a troublemaker.

After a whirlwind romance, they married in 1882 and had a son shortly after. Conflict quickly arose between them.

"This is a young woman who has a controlling, dour, respectable father, and she's been swept up by this man with aristocratic heritage who's a bit wild," Boucher says.

" But it turned out that she probably made the mistake I think many people have made … of trying to escape the rule of a patriarch and then ending up choosing another one instead. "

Nellie Melba started to dream of a life outside the colonies, Leigh Boucher says. (ABC Archives)

Melba found herself raising a child, mostly on her own, and rarely getting to perform. She decided to return to Melbourne, ostensibly to raise her son alongside her family.

Once in Melbourne, she worked with a new vocal coach to train her in the bel canto style, which was popular in Europe's concert halls.

In 1884, Melba made her professional debut at Melbourne Town Hall and it was a raging success.

"In Australian history, it was one of the most momentous debuts you could possibly imagine," Boucher says.

Melba leaves Melbourne

Melba's father finally appeared to support her ambitions. He had financed her singing classes and brought her to Europe where he was working, giving her a chance to pursue her operatic career.

But Melba's husband also went along.

"On the trip to London, Charles began to try and exert a lot of control over her. There are stories about her turning up at breakfast [on the boat over] with bruises on her face," Boucher says.

It's no wonder that on her arrival in London in 1886, abused by her husband, hampered by nerves and without the right clothes or accent, Melba flopped her pivotal audition at Covent Garden.

Undeterred, Melba travelled to Paris and became the student of German opera singer and teacher Mathilde Marchesi. She looked after her son and was barely scraping by.

"But Mathilde Marchesi identified Nellie as having a singular talent," Boucher says.

Marchesi was a maternal figure to the young singer; she improved her vocal technique but also taught her European etiquette and encouraged her to take on her stage name.

Mathilde Marchesi helped Nellie Melba work out how to make her way into the world of European opera, Leigh Boucher says. (ABC Archives)

"Together they came up with this identity that both harked back to her roots — Melba being Melbourne — but nonetheless, had an air of sophistication … it was not really a rebranding, I think, but a rebirth."

Melba debuted as an opera singer in Brussels in 1887 and picked up roles across Europe, making a name for herself playing mad women.

" She quickly became renowned as having a possibly once-in-a-generation voice … by 1890 she had broken through at London's Covent Garden, wiping the memory of that failed audition away. "

She also began an affair with Philippe, the Duke of Orleans, a dashing heir to the French throne.

Eventually, after Charles used the adultery as grounds for divorce and essentially abducted their son to Texas where he had relocated, the marriage was over. She didn't see her son for 12 years.

"She was not destroyed by the divorce, and she was not destroyed by the loss of her son. In fact, she sunk herself into work," Boucher says.

Farewell to Melba

Melba returned to Australia for a hugely successful tour in 1902.

"There were these amazing scenes of her returning to Melbourne and the streets being filled with thronging masses of people," Boucher says.

"Nellie was an Australian celebrity who not only was making it in Europe but was making it in European elite culture. She was proving that this was not a crass colony, but in fact a place of modernity."

One source said travelling with Nellie Melba during this tour was like "travelling through France with Marie-Antoinette". (Supplied: State Library of Queensland)

But after returning to London and, whipped up by the press who claimed she had been replaced, Melba stood in the wings and rudely outsang a rival at the Royal Opera House.

"In this moment, an emerging celebrity culture just got the better of her," Boucher says.

Melba regained her perch at the top of the opera hierarchy; beloved by the royal family, she had her own dressing room at Covent Garden.

Then in World War I, she raised money for the war effort by going on a US tour. There she was reunited with her son, but the tour was also plagued by strange accidents.

"Nellie became convinced that the Germans are out to get her because she was such a useful tool for the morale of the war efforts," Boucher says.

By the 1920s Melba was in her 60s and decided to retire. This is how the phrase "doing a Melba" was invented, as she spent many years giving farewell concerts.

It was on one of those many extended farewell tours that she contracted a fever. In 1931 she died quite suddenly in Sydney of septicaemia, a complication from what the press described as "facial surgery".

Boucher says, in a time without antibiotics, it was probably an early face lift.

" Her story is not reducible to this moment, but there is something in the ways in which she had to negotiate these gendered norms, negotiate the gendered restrictions of celebrity culture, and ended up dying from a face lift … that is tragic. It was a brutal end to an incredible life. "

Fans and the press across the globe mourned the death of Melba.

The New York Herald Tribune declared that she "was the last of those soprano empresses of song … Doubtless the gold age of song will return, but no Melba will sing for us again".

This article is based on research by Leigh Boucher.

title: Two Carlton AFL players hospitalised in Melbourne
text:
Two Carlton AFL football players have been hospitalised in Melbourne, the club says.

The club confirmed Lachie Cowan and Will Hayward were admitted to hospital on Sunday under separate circumstances.

Ambulance Victoria said advanced life-support paramedics responded to reports of an incident in South Yarra about 5:15am today.

"A man in his 20s was transported by road ambulance to The Alfred Hospital with upper body injuries in a stable condition," it said.

The club said Cowan received medical treatment and underwent observation, before being discharged a short time later.

Will Hayward experienced a minor cut to the head after a fall, and admitted himself to hospital, where he received stitches before being discharged, they added.

Cowan, a Tasmanian drafted to the Blues in 2022, has played 38 games for the club as a young defender.

Howard, who re-signed with Sydney in 2024, crossed over to the forward line at Carlton in 2025.



The club said it has been in regular contact with both players, with the priority on their wellbeing.

title: WA artist with cerebral palsy finds voice through painting
text:
On a quiet country road on Western Australia's south coast, Colin Hanssen is wrapping up his first exhibition.

Despite being a newcomer to the world of painting, there's been plenty to see on the walls, and floor, of the artist's rural Albany studio.

For Hanssen, who was born with cerebral palsy and is largely non-verbal, art has become a vital form of self expression.

The 31-year-old uses his wheelchair and right hand to blend colourful and earthy tones, combining performance with paint to create his abstract pieces.

Colin Hanssen's work is displayed in his Redmond studio, on the outskirts of Albany. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

His mother Wendy Hanssen said the unique skill was realised just six months ago in an art therapy class.

"That was when it was brought home that actually this could be an outlet for Colin," she said.

" This could potentially be his voice. "

Wendy Hanssen says painting is an outlet for her son, who is largely non-verbal. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

Beating the odds

His recent selection for this year's Southern Art and Craft Trail, an event which highlights talent across the region, shows just how much he has exceeded expectations, according to Ms Hanssen.

"We went and saw a neurosurgeon who told us to love Colin while we've got him, because he wasn't going to make it to his first birthday," she said.

"Colin's first birthday came and went, and we knew that we were clearly on the right track.

" Thirty-one years later, he's still with us, beating the odds left, right and centre. "

Colin Hanssen's paintings blend vibrant and earthy tones. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

A pre-verbal medium

Art therapist Serena McLaughlan has worked with Hanssen since he first started painting, and helped to curate the exhibition's collection.

"They [visitors] come in and they're just drawn to the work," she said.

"They're really interested in the story and fascinated by the process."

Serena McLaughlan is an art therapist based in the Great Southern. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

She said much of Hanssen's work draws from his time living in Africa.

"Engaging with vast expanses of landscape is a lived experience that comes through in the painting," she said.

"It's the power of art to talk of his lived experience and his stories over words.

" Art is pre-verbal — drawing, music and dance is all before words. "

Serena McLaughlan says many of Colin Hanssen's paintings draw on his lived experiences. (ABC Great Southern: Mark Bennett)

With the Art Trail completed, the team now has its sights set on the city.

"We've had two people, two artists from different galleries in Perth, asking if Colin will exhibit with them," Ms Hanssen said.

"We're going to look at getting a series done."

title: Gravel cycling championship brings global audience to tiny town
text:
A tiny town in southern Western Australia has become the first location outside Europe to hold an elite gravel cycling world championship.

Nannup, about 268 kilometres south of Perth, hosted thousands of cyclists and spectators this weekend for the 2026 UCI Gravel World Championships.

It was a major coup for the historic timber town, which is building its reputation as a mountain biking destination.

Crowds line the streets of Nannup for the Gravel World Championships. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

With the event expected to draw a global audience of up to 130 million people, Shire of Nannup Deputy President Vicki Hansen said securing it had taken years of work.

"Not many people even knew how to pronounce Nannup," she said.

"Now, Nannup, Western Australia is across the world."

Vicki Hansen says it took years of work to secure the event. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

The hills and forests surrounding the town have proven the ideal terrain for mountain biking, with Ms Hansen hopeful the event would showcase the local trails.

The event attracted almost 1,000 competitors from all over the world. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

"We want all these international riders, who didn't qualify, but have seen the event, to come on over," Ms Hansen said.

Competitors raced over two days, traversing courses of up to 144km through the Blackwood Valley.

Close to 1,000 cyclists are racing through the Blackwood Valley. (Supplied: SWPix)

"Nannup itself is only 70 metres above sea level but within a kilometre or less than that it suddenly increases to 300 metres above sea level," Shire President Tony Dean said.

"In that elevation … we've got the gravel itself."

Dutch cyclist Marianne Vos is the first person to win the gravel world championships twice. (Supplied: SWPix)

Dutch cyclist Marianne Vos took out the elite women's title in 4 hours and 30 minutes, followed by Germany's Rose Kloser and the Netherlands' Larisa Hartog.

It was the second championship victory for the two-time Olympic medallist.

Journey to Nannup

This year will be the fifth UCI Gravel World Championships event held, with previous events taking place in Italy and Belgium.

Wendy Oosterwoud, who travelled almost 30 hours from the Netherlands to compete in Nannup, said it was her first time outside of Europe.

"I think the flight was 21 hours, the drive to Amsterdam was almost two hours, [and] from Perth to Nannup was almost three," she said.

"I'm really happy to see this part of the world."

Wendy Oosterwoud says travelling to the Nannup gravel races was her first time outside Europe. (Supplied: Wendy Oosterwoud)

The Dutch cyclist has claimed seven podium titles, including winning the women's elite at a gravel world series in Poland this year.

She said the Nannup course was broader than those overseas.

"Here in Nannup, it's wide gravel roads," she said.

"But in the Netherlands … you have, I think, 200 corners, left right, left right."

Nils Lageman says the race is the most significant of its kind in the world. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

German cyclist Nils Lageman made the journey from his home near Cologne to compete in the 35-39 age group.

"The world championships were calling, and I just had to respond, wherever it is," he said.

"It looks great because of the nature."

US cyclists Tim Borsetti, Mark Litrell and John Steward had never heard of Nannup until the the event (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

Many international cyclists said they had never heard of Nannup, until the event, including US cyclist Tim Borsetti.

"I targeted this because I knew it would be an awesome event, because you guys have big wide roads like we do in the States," he said.

'Spreading the love'

With a regular population of about 1,000 people, accommodation in Nannup has been fully booked for the event.

Mr Dean said a tent city, and visitors staying in other nearby towns, had helped share the load.

Nannup welcomed the visiting cyclists and spectators with open arms. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

"We're spreading the love between Nannup and the rest of the South West," he said.

"With that many visitors, they're going to have to commute, unfortunately."

It has proven a win for some local businesses, with cafe owner Hayley Rubery registering one of the busiest days she could remember.

Tents and accommodation in surrounding communities helped Nannup handle the bumper crowds. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

"We had a 700 per cent increase in revenue to a normal Friday. It's insane," she said.

"We sold five days' worth of milk in one day, and we've never made more toasties in our entire lives."

Hayley Rubery says the event brought a 700 per cent jump in business. (ABC South West WA: Georgia Loney)

With the town's previous events leaning towards smaller-scale arts and culture festivals, Ms Rubery said they had been unsure what to expect.

"We prepped anyway and thank God we did."

title: Major US news networks face probe over White House coverage boycott
text:
US television networks are under investigation for potentially violating federal antitrust laws over decisions to boycott covering the White House following its decision to pull the credentials of reporters from three news organisations.

The US Justice Department said the networks under investigation include ABC, CBS, CNN, NBC and Fox News.

"Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act," a Justice Department spokesperson said.

"The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organisations have violated the antitrust laws."

Donald Trump has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news". (AP: Jacquelyn Martin)

The investigation is the latest in a series of clashes between the Trump administration and major news organisations.

Trump bans outlets from White House Cable networks CNN and MS NOW and newsletter publisher Politico have been banned from the White House, effective immediately, with more to follow, US President Donald Trump says.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly called the mainstream media "fake news" and frequently clashed with reporters.

The action also puts legal and potentially financial pressure on the media to continue coverage of the president even when they disagree with how the White House handles them.

The networks did not immediately respond to requests from Reuters for comment.

The New York Times was first to report about the probe.

The investigation comes after weeks of tension between the White House and the press.

Credentials revoked in September

On September 19, the White House blocked reporters from CNN, Politico, and MS NOW from entering the building, revoking their credentials.

The White House said covering the president was a "privilege — not a right".

The outlets sued the administration, alleging the exclusions violated the First Amendment and that the White House was retaliating over their coverage.

CNN is one of the five news organisations — along with ABC, CBS, Fox News and NBC — that make up the primary White House television pool.

Judge orders reversal of Trump's media ban A federal judge has ordered US President Donald Trump to restore White House access for journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

They share the costs of covering the president, take turns organising coverage and share the footage with outlets around the country.

All of the five television networks that cover the White House suspended coverage in solidarity and refused to provide replacement coverage.

The White House reinstated the credentials on September 24 after US District Judge Timothy Kelly ruled that the ban was likely unconstitutional and ordered the administration to "immediately return, reinstate, and restore" their access.

However, disputes over access to specific presidential events and pool assignments continued afterward.

Reuters

title: Running legend Kipchoge sets race record at Melbourne Marathon
text:
Eliud Kipchoge has lived up to his star billing at the Melbourne Marathon with a race-record performance.

Kenya's two-time Olympic champion and former world record holder has delighted several thousand fans at the MCG on Sunday morning with a dominating run.

Kipchoge broke away inside the last 10 kilometres of the 42.2km race and won in 2 hours 9 minutes 10 seconds — 2 seconds inside the previous race best.

He would have finished a few seconds quicker, but was waving to the crowd on the half-lap inside the MCG to the finish.

Thomas Do Canto was runner-up in 2:10:35 while fellow Australian Reece Edwards came third in 2:15:57.

In the women's race, New Zealand's Camille French was first to the tape in 2:28:25. Australia's Sinead Diver was 23 seconds back in second place, with Irish runner Nichola Sheridan a further 24 seconds back in third.

The 42km journey took participants down St Kilda Road, past Flinders Street Station, around Albert Park Lake, before a finish inside the MCG.

Kipchoge, 41, last won a marathon in 2023. He looked at the finish like it had been an easy training run, spending several minutes with fans alongside the MCG boundary line.

Kipchoge said it was a great feeling to finish at the famous stadium that also hosted the start and finish of the marathon at the 1956 Olympics — 70 years ago.

"So I come here to celebrate the 70 years and tell the people of Melbourne, 'Let us run together here at the MCG' so it was a beautiful time for me, happy to enter this stadium," Kipchoge said after the race.

This is only his second visit to Australia and his Melbourne Marathon debut.

It is part of Kipchoge's world tour, featuring a marathon on all seven continents, including Antarctica.

AAP/ABC

title: Albanese government's Pacific push leaves Cocos Island residents on the outer
text:
Residents of Australia's remotest territory say they feel forgotten by the government's global climate change efforts ahead of the major COP31 forum in Türkiye.

The federal government hosted pre-COP meetings in Tuvalu and Fiji this week in a bid to raise the voices of Pacific Island nations.

But on the far opposite side of Australia's recognised territory, and 8,900km from this week's Pacific meetings, residents of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands (CKI) feel they have been left in the lurch.

Tuvalu (pictured) and Cocos (Keeling) Islands face similar climate threats like flooding and coastal erosion. (Supplied)

Faced with coastal erosion, flooding and other climate-driven issues mirroring those of Pacific nations, the Cocos Islanders made a bid to be represented at COP31.

Their application was approved by the United Nations, but not selected for funding by the Australian government, with the delegation informed they had been unsuccessful just before this week's talks.

Their panel proposal, submitted by the University of Western Australia's Oceans Institute, would have featured the challenges faced by the Cocos (Keeling) Islands as a low-lying island community.

The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are facing coastal erosion and flooding, like their Pacific Island counterparts. (Supplied: Chris Bray)

Residents rue missed opportunity

Home Island resident Luluk Sloan said COP31 presented an opportunity to bring global awareness to the Cocos (Keeling) Islands.

With a coastal hazard management plan suggesting retreat slammed by the islands' residents, they had hoped attendance would have allowed them to learn how other island communities were dealing with climate-driven challenges.

"A council delegation was actually looking at visiting the Pacific Islands just to see what sort of mitigation they've got planned in terms of not retreating," she said.

"I think it's a disappointment that we don't have that link; we can't really tell our story globally."

Luluk Sloan lives on Home Island. (Supplied: Luluk Sloan)

Ms Sloan said it felt like the islands were being left behind.

" We are an Australian territory, who's voicing for us? Who's vouching for us? No-one. "

West Island resident Rose Cummins also would have attended the conference.

"I certainly applaud the Pacific Islands. I think they've done an incredible job in raising the profile of climate change and how it's directly impacting them," Ms Cummins said.

"I guess we would just like the same opportunity."

Rose Cummins lives on West Island. (Supplied: Rose Cummins)

A spokesperson for the Department of Climate Change, Energy and Water acknowledged the impact climate change was having on the Islands.

But the department rejected suggestions that the focus on the Pacific came at the expense of Australian communities.

"Engagement with Pacific partners complements, rather than replaces, our support for Australian communities facing climate risks," the spokesperson said.

The Oceans Institute said it remained committed to working with the islands' community to help address the ongoing challenges posed by climate change.

Community not heard

Residents say there has been a lack of meaningful consultation on the plan to manage the islands' ongoing coastal risks.

"I think a lot of people felt that it's another consultation," Ms Sloan said.

"What are they going to do about it? Possibly, probably, nothing."

Cocos (Keeling) Islands residents say they have seen metres of shoreline vanish. (Supplied: Luluk Sloan)

Ms Cummins said expressions of interest for a community reference group, promised since the start of the year, were only issued last month.

"There's no decision-making abilities; it won't affect any policy or anything like that," she said.

"That will still be done by experts who don't live here."

The Climate Change Department spokesperson said the Coastal Hazard Risk Management and Adaptation Plan (CHRMAP) was a key step in supporting CKI to respond and adapt to climate change.

"The [plan] gives us a clear picture of the coastal hazards facing the islands and will help guide the work we do together to strengthen preparedness and improve community safety," the spokesperson said.

But Ms Sloan remained sceptical.

"I think people are slowly realising that … the delivery of services is on the decline," she said.

"And that's probably because they're thinking: 'Oh yeah, 50 years from now, the islands are going to go under.'"

title: Pro surfer swaps California waves for life in the outback
text:
Last month, Brazilian professional surfer Caio Ibelli was riding barrelling waves at the Surfing Champions Trophy in the Maldives.

Today, he's at home, in the outback, almost 1,000 kilometres from the east coast.

The 32-year-old is one of Mount Isa's newest residents, swapping surf and sand for the red dirt plains of north-west Queensland.

Caio Ibelli's days are now spent wrangling his toddler in the outback town of Mount Isa. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"After living in so many different places, this is the best place in the world to live," Ibelli said.

Originally from Brazil, Ibelli moved to Australia after a stint in California.

First picking up a surfboard when he was three years old, he said by the time he was seven, his talent was being noticed.

Caio Ibelli was three years old when he started surfing in Brazil. (Supplied: Caio Ibelli)

By 23, Ibelli had qualified for the World Surf League tour, kicking off a nine-year professional career.

"After that, I kind of retired … I wanted to have kids and a family," he said.

Ibelli said although a move to the outback wasn't always planned, he was proud to be raising his son in the city, despite knowing little about what to expect.

One-year-old Thomas Ibelli is spending his first years in the outback, despite his dad's professional surfing career. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"It is getting a little bit too hot. It's about 38 degrees right now, and I heard it goes all the way to 46 … I've never felt that in my life," he said.

It was his wife's career that brought the family, including their one-year-old son, Thomas, to the region after completing her medical degree.

"Every time I speak with my friends in the hospital and say that my husband is a professional surfer, everybody has the same reaction… 'Oh, how?'" Talie Ibelli laughed.

"We actually love it here. We love the community, and it's a great opportunity for my son to be raised here … this is the real Australia."

Caio Ibelli won the World Surfing Championships in the Maldives last month. (Supplied: Caio Ibelli)

The family have only been to the beach about six times since moving to the bush, which makes his recent win in the Maldives all the more impressive.

"I was playing with my son and then my phone rang and I'm like, 'What? Go to the Maldives in 10 days? I'm smelling the dirt here right now,'" he said.

He said muscle memory along with his new-found "outback attitude" helped him snag the overall win.

"The event was cool. Winning it was amazing, it was awesome," he said.

Caio Ibelli spent about a decade travelling the world surfing circuit. (Supplied: Caio Ibelli)

"Seeing my son playing on the blue water, watching the sharks all day, it was just super special."

Mount Isa has its fair share of athletic prowess, with tennis star Pat Rafter, golfer Greg Norman and AFL player Charlie Cameron all born in the city.

It's unclear yet whether Caio Ibelli's son, Thomas, will follow in his father's footsteps. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

Ibelli said it was a privilege to be among the mining city's claims to fame, including perhaps being its most famous surfer.

"After I won the contest in the Maldives, coming back to Mount Isa, I've been going around in places, and people are like, 'Are you the surfer?' And I'm like, 'Yeah', and people are kind of tripping," he said.

The Ibelli family have found a home in north-west Queensland, living in the mining city of Mount Isa. (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"I feel so fortunate to be here, Australia is such a good place, and Mount Isa is amazing."

Even with the positives, he admits it is tough to be a surfer with no surf.

"I'm really missing some kind of water, so sometimes I go to swim, or I'm just hoping Mount Isa Council will build us a wave pool sometime soon," he laughed.

Ibelli's next dream is teaching bush kids how to surf.

Caio and Talie Ibelli plan on raising Thomas as an "Aussie kid". (ABC News: Abbey Halter)

"I'm so grateful for being here with my family, and I feel like the least I could do is like giving back, and I would love to some day take local people to the beach and surf," he said.

" Who knows, like one day we can bring like a Mount Isa Surf Club on a competition. "

title: Taylor says he would welcome return of Frydenberg to politics
text:
Opposition Leader Angus Taylor says he would welcome the return of former Liberal treasurer Josh Frydenberg to politics, as he continues to defend the Coalition's newly released migration policy.

On Saturday, Mr Frydenberg released excerpts of his upcoming memoir A Grateful Son, published in The Australian, which included details of his election defeat four years ago.

The former Kooyong MP, who was a leadership frontrunner, fuelled speculation he may contest a seat in the next election as he outlined his vision for Australia.

He urged the Liberal Party to "reclaim" the centre of politics, arguing there was a lack of political courage in Canberra.

Mr Frydenberg proposed several policy changes across energy and AI and a pitch to leverage a portion of state GST revenue based on how many homes were built.

Josh Frydenberg says Canberra lacks political courage. (AAP: James Ross)

When asked whether he would welcome or fear his former colleague's return, Mr Taylor said he needed "every good leader" heading into the next federal election.

"People will play different roles … whether it's just liking Facebook and Instagram posts all the way through to being a candidate," he told Insiders on Sunday.

"But we've all got to mobilise, and I welcome Josh playing whatever role he's able to play."

Coalition policy for 100,000 NOM The Coalition would cut net overseas migration to 100,000 for two years.

Mr Taylor immediately added that the Coalition would not adopt Mr Frydenberg's suggestion of raising the GST.

"We will not be raising the GST in the middle of a cost-of-living crisis. That we won't do," he said.

"We'll put Australia and Australians first, but we won't be raising taxes.



"I'm a fiscal conservative. I believe in lower taxes, and that's why we'll be giving the tax-back guarantee, lower income taxes for Australians without raising the GST."

Taylor defends budget neutrality of Coalition's migration cuts

Despite economic concerns raised by the business, aged care, education and construction sectors about the Coalition's migration policy, the opposition leader maintained it would be "budget neutral".

Mr Taylor said the policy had not been officially costed by the Parliamentary Budget Office, due to "constraints".

"In terms of analysis, there are limitations on what the parliamentary office can do because of its legislation. It cannot model directly on Labor's policies so we had to give it assumptions to work with," he said.

"That is a constraint, but as we approach the election, we won't have that constraint."

The policy proposes slashing temporary migration by 650,000 places over four years and offsetting the lost tax revenue with 100,000 additional skilled migrants, who would be higher-paid and therefore pay more tax.

Compare Labor, the Coalition and One Nation's migration cuts One Nation wants negative migration in its first years, the Coalition has promised to more than halve it, while Labor has announced measures to ensure migration actually falls to its target of 225,000.

He reiterated that aged care, which heavily relies on temporary visas, would be subject to a transitional arrangement that allowed these workers to stay on existing visas for a longer period of time.

"If you cut numbers and raise standards, you can maintain budget neutrality. And you can strengthen the economy because the average income, the average productivity of the person coming into this country rises," he said.

"What's happening under Labor is they are driving economic growth through population growth alone."

Australia's net overseas migration, or NOM, fell to 292,100 people in the year to March, with Labor pursuing a target of 245,000 for this financial year and 225,000 the year after.

Tanya Plibersek says the Coalition needs to go back to the drawing board with its migration policy. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek labelled Mr Taylor's interview a "car crash" and questioned why he could not provide full economic modelling.

"It's disappointing that a once major party of government can't answer basic questions about the economic impact of their policies," she said.

"If you can unite big business and small businesses and farmers and unions, saying your policy will smash the economy, maybe it's time to go back to the drawing board."

Meanwhile, Immigration Minister Tony Burke has warned that bridging visa cuts at the scale proposed by the Coalition would require billions of dollars in infrastructure and workforce investment.

"They need to let us know how many beds, how many compliance officers, and where the new detention centres are going," Mr Burke told News24.

"The numbers they are talking about, we are talking billions and billions of dollars I suspect."

title: More than 70 stranded as Solomon Islands ferry drifts for days
text:
More than 70 passengers have been stranded aboard a drifting ferry in Solomon Islands waters since Friday, as an international operation scrambles to get supplies to the vessel.

The ferry was sailing between the remote islands of Anuta and Vanikoro in Temotu Province when its engine failed on Friday, leaving it adrift at sea.

A Panama-registered bulk carrier reached MV Awka on Sunday morning and began transferring water and food, passenger John Tua said.

The Solomon Islands Maritime Authority told the ABC there are 74 passengers and 16 crew on board.

Mr Tua, a nurse with the provincial government, said the engine was overheating when it broke down about 100 nautical miles from its destination.

"Everyone is OK, no-one panicked, passengers were calm … we're just waiting for the rescue ships to come," he said.

While the seas have been mostly calm, Mr Tua said the ship had also experienced rough swells.

A distress call was issued on Friday, with the Solomon Islands enlisting help from the Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) and New Caledonian government.

John Tua with communication equipment dropped from an Australian aircraft. (Supplied: John Tua)

An AMSA spokesperson said its Cairns-based rescue jet made several drops of critical items including food, water, medical supplies and communications equipment.

A French aircraft from New Caledonia was first on the scene on Saturday, dropping life rafts and desalination equipment.

"The urgent need was water. We've run out of water onboard … the ship's water supply was used to cool the engine down when it was heating up," Mr Tua said.

"We have lots of brown coconuts on board to drink, but our water is finished."

A Temotu provincial government statement said: "The latest information indicates that the passengers on board MV Akwa now have access to essential supplies, including drinking water, food, and medical provisions delivered through the air and sea supply operations."

On Sunday morning, the Panama-registered bulk carrier Sunnine 3 reached the vessel early and began transferring water and food, which was live-streamed online by Mr Tua.

Loading...

Passengers have stayed in touch with families using the ship's Starlink internet, while Mr Tua has been the main source of news for worried relatives.

Temotu Premier Stanley Tehiahua said a police patrol boat was on its way from Honiara.

"To all relatives, families and friends anxiously awaiting news of their loved ones, we recognise the emotional distress and uncertainty you are experiencing," he said in a statement.

"We call on everyone to remain calm, united and prayerful during this difficult time," Mr Tehiahua said.

The ABC has requested comment from the Solomon Islands Maritime Safety Administration and the country's Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre.

The incident comes four weeks after the inter-island ferry MV Matui sank in rough seas in neighbouring Vanuatu with more than 50 people onboard. Two people have since been confirmed dead, 14 have been rescued while 39 others remain missing.

There have been calls for Australia and New Zealand to invest more in maritime safety, including from Peter Nuttall, technical adviser for the Micronesian Centre for Sustainable Transport at the University of the South Pacific, who told the ABC after the Matui sinking that Australia could easily invest in better vessels for the Pacific.

"We could have built 40 to 60 safe, brand new, low-carbon ferries for the same budget as we've spent on 20-something patrol boats, several which have already been scrapped," Dr Nuttall said.

title: I thought no-one would love me, but Jed shows up in ways I never thought possible
text:
Chanelle Morris thought she was going to be "alone forever" after many deflating and hurtful dating experiences because of her vision impairment.

The 27-year-old had all but given up on finding love when she caught the eye of Jed on a social outing at a driving range.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

These are Chanelle and Jed's words.

People didn't understand my disability

Chanelle: I have a type of chorioretinal dystrophy, a rare vision condition which impacts my peripheral vision and ability to notice detail.

I'm legally blind in one eye and the other one is not that much better.

I thought no-one would love me because of my condition.

Chanelle says having a vision impairment made dating difficult. (Supplied)

I thought that I was too much for people. I feel like a lot of people with disability experience that.

Something that really rocked my confidence was when I would speak to someone, it would appear that my eyes were focused behind them, not on them.

So I stopped approaching people in public settings.

I used to get anxious in the lead-up to meeting someone from a dating app because I chose not to disclose my vision condition. It led to some people not believing me when I told them, or worse, being the subject of blind jokes that were disrespectful.

Once I included my condition in my dating profile, I got fewer matches, but they were more authentic, genuine and open.

I just didn't think that anyone would accept my vision impairment because most people didn't understand it and there was a lot of fear around it.

I couldn't see he was checking me out

Chanelle: I was hosting a women's golf event at a driving range on the Gold Coast and Jed just happened to be there that day.

Our meet-cute is a funny story because he was checking me out, but I couldn't see that.

One of the ladies I was there with noticed and actually went over to Jed to see if he was single and was interested in me.

She came charging over to me and said, "Go right now, he's interested."

I wrote my number on a drink coaster and went straight over, and I can't remember what I said, I just remember the adrenaline. I gave him my number and then I left because it was at the end of the event.

But I left my golf clubs behind because I was so nervous.

So I sent one of my friends back to get them because I was like, "I'm not going back in there."

Chanelle and Jed's meet-cute was at a driving range. (Supplied)

I remember Jed texted me that day to organise a date two days later.

I was so nervous, I couldn't eat.

But he was so sweet and texted me specific instructions on where he was sitting at the restaurant so I could find him.

I'd never had anyone do that for me before.

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

Jed: When I went to the driving range, I thought I'd go hit some golf balls on my day off. Little did I know I'd find the love of my life.

Jed says Chanelle's vision impairment was never a barrier to them dating. (Supplied)

I was definitely checking Chanelle out.

The first thing her friend said to me was, "She's keen on you but she has an eye condition."

So I knew about her vision impairment straight away.

But it wasn't something that was going to change my mind or affect my decision to see her.

I was pretty nervous before our date, but it couldn't have gone any better, the conversation flowed so well.

I just love how caring and supportive she is.

My heart is healing

Jed: I have type 1 diabetes and Chanelle will get me some sugar if I need it because my sugar's low or she carries my insulin pen for me in her purse.

I think that's why we get on so well, because we know what it's like to need support and help.

I've always admired her selflessness.

She has so much time for other people, including me.

She goes to conferences for motivational speaking and I am so proud and impressed by that.

I'll come home, and she's got some sort of little surprise for me.

I've never felt so at ease before in my life.

Chanelle and Jed say the support they show one another has deepened their love. (Supplied)

Chanelle: He shows up for me in a way that I didn't even know was possible and he says to me that I do the same for him.

The main thing I can't do with my vision impairment is drive, so Jed drives me a lot, which is great.

Every time we go to a restaurant or a cafe, he reads the menu without me even asking or helps me read labels at the grocery store.

He's like my eyes for anything, even helping me find the bathroom when we're out, which is a big anxiety for people with low vision.

Jed's my caddy at my golf competitions now, so he's literally my eyes.

We'll practise at the golf range now and as soon as he's not looking, I can't hit the ball.

I need him to help me play.

I can really be myself and I love that.

He makes me feel like a whole person and I'm more than enough for him.

My heart is healing in ways I never expected, and I could not be more grateful.

title: The $10 pint is extinct – this is what you can expect to pay for a beer in every capital city
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If you’ve ever done a double-take at the cost of buying a round of beers for your mates at the pub these days, your complaints have been justified: since January 2020, the average price of a pint of beer has risen by nearly $1 every 18 months, or from $9.96 to $13.76 across the nation. And if you’re in Melbourne, tough luck; you’re typically paying more than the rest of the country for Australia’s favourite beers, according to exclusive data provided by Square. Click on the interactive below to see how prices compare for your beer of choice across capital cities. Some pricing information is missing due to insufficient data in some cities, including Carlton Dry and Carlton Draught in Brisbane, and Carlton Draught and Balter XPA in Adelaide. City-level pint comparison data for VB, Asahi, Furphy and Heaps Normal was incomplete and has been excluded from the final data set. A pint of Balter XPA costs more in Melbourne ($15.70) than any other Australian city on average. The same goes for Guinness ($15.51), Carlton Draught ($13.91), Carlton Dry ($12.86) and Great Northern Super Crisp ($12.95). Meanwhile, the opposite is true for those who live in Perth, which is generally the cheapest capital city to buy a pint of those beers. “That to me suggests [those beers are] trying to do some sort of targeted discounting or trying to break in to the Western Australia market,” said beer expert and The Crafty Pint founder James Smith. “WA as a whole, in terms of hospitality and the beer production industry, has generally held firm longer than other states did.”

Advertisement

Related Article Alcohol Think Gen Z is to blame for alcohol’s decline? Think again The steepest increases came after pandemic lockdowns ended in 2022, after which most pint prices rose by about 10 per cent, said Square executive David Schnabl. “Most [pubs] held prices for as long as they could, which is why pub beer may have felt like it lagged the grocery aisle in the early inflation years,” he said. “Increases have moderated every year since, but they’ve never reversed.” The national average price of premium beers Balter XPA ($14.53) and Guinness ($14.48) have been drifting towards the $15 mark. “Craft beer was already trading at a premium, but the gap between premium and mainstream has continued to widen. The $10 pint is effectively extinct in this dataset,” said Schnabl. “Even XXXX Gold, the cheapest pint of any beer we tracked, now averages $11.24 nationally.” The Balter XPA (extra pale ale) gained popularity for being an approachable craft beer. Beer breakdown

Advertisement

Stone & Wood Pacific Ale tends to be the most consistently priced across the country, with less than $1 difference between the cheapest and most expensive city, Sydney ($14.25) and Adelaide ($15.23). Residents of Adelaide, where Coopers Brewery originated, are paying more than others to drink a Coopers Pale Ale at $13.81 (with the exception of Perth). A pint of Great Northern ($11.73), Australia’s best-selling beer, has risen more than any other major tap beer, at 43 per cent since 2020, when it was $8.21. Guinness (which has enjoyed a cultural resurgence thanks to the viral trend of “splitting the G”) is not far behind, increasing 41 per cent from $10.25 to $14.48 a pint. What’s the most you’ve paid for a pint in Australia? Let us know in the comments. Publicans in Victoria are grappling with more levies and taxes than those in some other states, including the mental health wellbeing levy and the COVID-19 debt repayment payroll tax, which impact venues where payroll exceeds $10 million. Meanwhile, higher land tax and council rates as well as stricter licensing conditions, which include a mandatory guard-to-patron ratio for late night venues, have also pushed up overheads and squeezed margins. “I certainly hear my mates who’ve got pubs say: ‘They’re f---ing killing us here,’” said Smith. But the popularity of Carlton Draught as the state’s most ordered tap beer endures.

Advertisement

Pros: delicious. Cons: increasingly expensive. iStock “I reckon there could be an element in Victoria or in Melbourne, people knowing we can charge more because people are going to buy it anyway. They might walk away from the bar and go, ‘I can’t believe how much it’s cost me for a round’, but they’re never going to look at anything else on tap.” Related Article Beer and cider From ‘splitting the G’ to the perfect pour: Eight things you need to know about Guinness Perth’s prices also appear cheaper as there’s a more “entrenched pint culture” on the west coast than the east coast, according to Titanium Property food and retail planning expert Taylor Westlake. About 8 per cent of greater Perth’s population was born in England, where pints are the standard beer size (570ml), compared with greater Sydney’s 2.9 per cent. A schooner (425ml) is the default drink size in NSW. “Pints are charged at a premium in NSW and Queensland, compared to the base price of a schooner (425ml),” said Westlake. “In Perth, its more common for a pint to be the base beer price – the fact they are more common could have kept its price down over time.” And in South Australia, a “pint” measures at 425ml, which is a schooner everywhere else; and if you order a schooner in Adelaide, you’ll get a Sydney middy (285ml). Taxed for drinking

Advertisement

Australia has the world’s third-highest alcohol tax rate in the world. One of the biggest factors pushing up beer prices is the twice-yearly alcohol excise increase, which is tied to inflation. Since 2000, beer prices have risen by about 27 per cent after general inflation has been factored in, according to AMP analysis. “In Australia prices have gone up by 113 per cent over the period, but beer prices have gone up a lot more, meaning that’s a real increase in beer prices,” said AMP economist My Bui. “In other words, the nominal increase in beer prices is almost 170 per cent, [so] the real change in beer prices has been about 27 per cent.” Last year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese made much noise of taking the pressure off beer prices by freezing the excise on draught beer for two years. “[It’s] a commonsense measure that is good for beer drinkers, good for brewers and good for pubs,” he said in March last year. But the temporary freeze is only for the draught (or tap) beer market, 90 per cent of which is controlled by the two foreign Big Alcohol multinationals: Lion, a subsidiary of $21 billion Japanese beverage conglomerate Kirin, and CUB, a subsidiary of Japanese rival Asahi. “All the freeze is doing is giving producers a little breathing room to either not increase prices or to absorb the cost. It will not have any impact on the cost and/or price of beer now,” said Independent Brewers Association chief executive Kylie Lethbridge.

You need to be at the same level when you train with them, so you’re working more hard than them because you’re young.” Related Article Socceroos The curious stat that illustrates Socceroos young gun’s quality Postolachi was just 13 when he arrived at PSG. The Moldovian striker eventually joined fellow French Ligue 1 outfit Lille, where he shared the pitch with Portuguese sensations Jose Fonte and Renato Sanches. But after then taking his talents to Belgium and Romania, the 26-year-old has set his sights on a new challenge: restoring Brisbane Roar to the champion status they enjoyed last decade. Not since the 2020-21 season have the three-time A-League winners featured in the finals race, with the glory days of their trio of titles between the 2010-11 and 2013-14 seasons now a distant memory.

Advertisement

That run of early exits appeared to be on the cusp of ending during their last campaign, before Socceroos defender Lucas Herrington’s transfer to the Colorado Rapids – a move that then inspired his lucrative venture to the Premier League with Hull City. From that point, the Roar would win just once from their remaining 14 clashes. But it was the club’s passionate drive to return to the top that captivated Postolachi and drew him to Australia. “I love the mentality they have in Brisbane. We want this year to do better than last year, to arrive as the top team of Australia, and this motivation is good for me,” he said. Tyrese Francois brings Premier League experience to the Brisbane Roar. “It was a new challenge for me, a new country, new teammates – everything new. I was surprised by the quality of the players we have in the team. Also, the guys have accepted me so fast, and I got used to the training really fast, and adapted really fast.”

Advertisement

In a bid to restore the fallen contenders, coach Michael Valkanis has swept change through his squad. Postolachi is joined by former Fulham midfielder Tyrese Francois, four-time Socceroos defender Joel King, South Korea veteran Nam Tae-hee, and new skipper Tom Aldred as the fresh faces to spearhead Brisbane back to the top. Related Article Socceroos Irankunda senses a dominant decade beckons. Brazil will test that theory “We want to dominate more with the ball this season, that’s no secret. To do that, you need the types of players like Tyrese, like Nam, like Joel being a defender who’s very comfortable with the ball,” Valkanis said. “It’s not just dominating possession for the sake of it, but to be able to create opportunities to score goals. A lot of these players have good mobility and speed, so that’s very important in the A-League, and most of all, they’re the type of characters and people we brought in who will put the team first.” Francois said his “unbelievable” experience growing up in the Fulham system forced him to “grow up really quickly”, given how competitive the sport’s landscape was in England, and how young athletes were thrust into intensive training and competition.

Advertisement

Injuries, however, left him at a crossroads, and despite featuring at Socceroos camps in 2022, he is yet to land on the international stage. But the former Olyroos captain believes he is ready to rediscover his best. “Of course, it’s a dream of mine to play for the Socceroos, but I also understand it’s one step at a time, and the most important step for me right now is to do my best for the Brisbane Roar,” Francois admitted. Loading “I was at a point in my career where I needed a reset. I had some unbelievable experiences abroad, but the last two years have been very difficult for me. I needed a new environment, I needed a new home that would allow me to progress and also do what I know I can do. “Every footballer wants to play, and when you can’t play, you kind of feel useless. You learn very quickly over there that it’s not personal – if you can’t play, you’re not needed in the team.

Advertisement

“I just needed to come back and enjoy my football again – enjoy playing football with a smile on my face and, naturally, my best football will come out.” Postolachi felt the European exposure he and Francois brought would be the tonic needed to arrest Brisbane’s slide and ensure their freefall would not happen again. “We come from Europe, and in Europe there’s relegation, so you fight to keep your place in the first league. This is different, but we want to bring this competitiveness to never lose a game,” he said. “It’s not like, ‘OK, next time we’ll get a chance’. You need to be a winner every time.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. Sign up for our Morning Edition newsletter.

title: Pearl Harbour and Hawaii’s connection to Qantas’ Double Sunrise
text:

BusinessCompaniesAviation Pearl Harbour and Hawaii’s connection to Qantas’ Double Sunrise Chris Zappone October 11, 2026 — 2:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. On a warm January day in Hawaii in early 1941, a flying boat appeared on the horizon over the sea, and landed in the water outside Honolulu. The plane - a Consolidated PBY Catalina – made its landing on January 27, it had departed from San Diego, where it was built, and it had just accomplished a rare feat. It had spent “almost a full day in the air” traversing 4392km to get to Hawaii. Waiting in Honolulu was a Qantas crew. On July 10, 1943, the first ‘Double Sunrise’ Catalina flight departs Perth for Ceylon (Sri Lanka). This remains the longest scheduled passenger service in the world by elapsed time. Honolulu is where Qantas took its first delivery of the long-range planes that the “Flying Kangaroo” would later enable the Double Sunrise flights - at a distance of 6480 km between Perth and Ceylon, keeping Australia connected with the UK during World War II. Within months of the first plane’s delivery, the Imperial Japanese Navy would stage its infamous surprise attack on US military bases in Hawaii, and the US would declare war on Japan and Germany.

Advertisement

But in early 1941, when the first Catalina plane was to be delivered to Qantas, the US was still neutral, while Australia, with links to the UK, was already at war. The Catalina PBY-6A became the lifeline which helped keep Qantas alive and maintained communications between Australia and the United Kingdom. As a result, the delivery flight “had to be flown by an American crew and that legal title would be transferred to Qantas in Honolulu,” according to academic Silvano Jung. Despite the RAAF pilots being seconded to Qantas, “the aircraft also had to be marked with civilian registration”. Designated VH-AFA, the Australian crew included famed aviator Captain P.G. Taylor. Two days later, the plane left for Canton Island - roughly between Hawaii and Fiji. VH-AFA arrived at Rose Bay, Sydney on February 2, 1941. The delivery flight from Hawaii to Sydney was only the third time the Pacific had been crossed by air. To get from Hawaii to Sydney safely in 1941 required flight crews to use a combination of dead reckoning (calculating location from fixed points), radio direction finding and astronomical navigation, with the Catalina’s blister bubble on top, designed for this purpose.

Advertisement

Japanese forces specifically targeted the PBY Catalinas during the Pearl Harbour attack on December 7, 1941. US Navy photograph But these three methods themselves had to be continually cross-checked to ensure reliability. The Catalina was made for the original Double Sunrise route, connecting Western Australia to Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and onwards to London. The Double Sunrise flights began in 1943, as Japanese forces advanced through South-East Asia, towards Australia. Today, the legacy of those flights lives on in Qantas’ upcoming Project Sunrise project, which is poised to redefine long-haul travel, even as, like in the 1940s, geopolitical uncertainty returns. Right equipment in the right hands Finding the right aircraft for the mission is a recurring theme of the displays at Honolulu’s Pearl Harbour Aviation Museum, home to iconic planes like the B-25 Mitchell and Japanese Mitsubishi A6M “Zero.” The museum recounts Japan’s surprise attack and the Pacific War that followed.

Advertisement

Ultimately, World War II came down to the right equipment in the right hands – and the PBY Catalina was a prime example – in its use by Qantas, but also the RAAF, and the US Navy. The Douglas SBD-2P Dauntless dive bomber, on display at the Pearl Harbor Aviation Museum. It was used in the Battle of the Coral Sea, which relieved the threat to the supply lines between the US and Australia. The Age Beyond civilian transport in Qantas livery, the Catalina military planes played a vital role in patrolling Australia’s vast borders, and they operated across the Pacific as an observation and reconnaissance aircraft. The RAAF ordered 253 of them. As a museum docent, Scott Mensen explained to me, the Catalinas made up patrol fleets in the Pacific during World War II “so they could operate from remote locations because they didn’t need a runway. “Since they could land in the water at any small island they could easily fly to them, and they could fly missions out of those islands.

Advertisement

“They were based all over the Pacific, and they had units that basically took care of the servicing of the aircraft that they could return to.” Recognising their role as the “eyes of the fleet”, the Japanese targeted the Catalinas parked at Pearl Harbour during the attack on December 7 1941. By the time the attack had finished, only 11 of the 61 Catalinas across the island of Oahu were airworthy. One patrol squadron of 12 saw seven of its planes destroyed. US military commanders had grouped them together to guard against potential sabotage by local Japanese spies, which inadvertently made the planes easier targets. A Mitsubishi A6M “Zero” on display at the Pearl Harbour Aviation Museum. The long-range fighter saw action through the Pacific Chris Zappone/The Age Even today in Australia, the legacy of the PBY is evident, as the plane is featured in museums nationwide – from the Qantas founder museum to the Aviation Heritage Museum in Perth. There’s even a monument to the PBY patrols in Cairns.

Advertisement

There is a cluster of Catalina wrecks in Broome that can be visited. A museum in Victoria for the wartime flying boat repair depot in Lake Boga. The hybrid fuselage-hull, dual prop engines mounted over the massive wings and the bulging blister windows out the side are a reminder of how design is shaped by needs. Qantas Catalina flying boat at Karachi in 1945. Alamy Stock Photo In the museum, the individual stories of planes correlate to specific battles. The Battle of Midway turned the tide against the Japanese, the Battle of the Coral Sea relieved the threat to the supply lines between the US and Australia. The museum also highlights how in a crunch, militaries and economies had to scramble to innovate, and – to use a contemporary word – iterate new versions of aircraft. The B-25 Mitchell had to be stripped down and lightened to allow it to conduct the first US bombing raid on Japan, for example. Designers, engineers, and welders worked non-stop to make the changes needed for a mission. Some planes would succeed, while others got consigned to history books (The Brewster F2A Buffalo fighter, anyone?)

Advertisement

Technological progress is rarely a straight line. Radar transformed war in both the Pacific and Europe. Today a Japanese Self-Defence Force member takes a picture of the Ford Island Control Tower. The Age/ Chris Zappone However, in December 1941, radar was a new technology that was not operated continuously. On the morning of December 7, US radar operators detected incoming Japanese aircraft, but officers mistook the signal for a flight of incoming American B-17 bombers from the mainland. The evolving situation of 1941 gives the aviation engineering on display at the museum a poignancy. It also begs the question in our time about what might be the right machines for this era (Ghost Bat? Ghost Shark? Virginia-class subs?)

Advertisement

The correct mix is seemingly one of hardware, lots of software, and humans who can use the technology effectively. Culture, design and war While many aviation museums assemble the odds and ends that are available and put them on display, the Pearl Harbour Aviation Museum boasts a more coherent collection. And the museum had, to me at least, a kind of energy to it, one that can sometimes be absent for aviation museums featuring historical planes. Of course, the Pearl Harbour museum also has the advantage of place. The attack took place on Ford Island. From Ford Island Control Tower, visitors can see with their own eyes the landscape (and airspace) that the Imperial Japanese Navy attacked in 1941. The destroyer USS Shaw explodes after being hit by bombs during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour, Hawaii on December 7, 1941. AP

Advertisement

And in fact, the museum sits directly across the water from active base Naval Station Pearl Harbour. Given the sensitive nature of the military bases, visitors without active military ID can only get to the museum by parking at the visitor centre and taking a free bus on to Ford Island. The proximity between history and the present is everywhere. The museum’s CEO is ex-Blue Angel pilot John Hiltz, who, until not so long ago, was flying F/A-18F off aircraft carriers. The museum is nestled in a hive of activity with military planes and ships passing by. Its displays in this setting are a reminder that history, well, it happens sometimes. In 1941, the Americans had based their Pacific fleet in Pearl Harbour on the hunch that Japan would attack further southwest in the Pacific, nearer Australia. The Grumman F4F-3 Wildcat fighter used by the US Marines at Wake Island, the Battle of Coral Sea, and the Battle of Midway. The Age/ Chris Zappone

Advertisement

Instead, a Japanese taskforce set sail in radio silence across a northern route and surprised the US, in an attempt to cripple the entire US fleet. Nearby in the waters surrounding Ford Island lies the USS Arizona Memorial, the resting place for over 1102 service members killed during the surprise assault. Despite its serious, even solemn history, the Pearl Harbour Aviation Museum also celebrates the culture and design and even music of the 1940s - and is friendly to kids and families. The site attracts a wide audience, including families, active-duty military personnel from local bases, and, when I visited, uniformed members of Japan Self-Defence Forces, with rising sun patches on their sleeves, also on site. The ‘Double Sunrise’ Catalinas being serviced on the ramp at Nedlands on the Swan River, with Vega Star in the foreground during WWII. Courage in the Skies (Allen & Unwin, 2017) Australian visitors often take special interest in relics recovered from nearby regions, such as a Nakajima B5N “Kate” torpedo bomber retrieved from Rabaul, Papua New Guinea.

Advertisement

Displayed outside on the tarmac are additional aircraft with Pacific service history, including a Royal Australian Air Force F-111 wearing its full military markings. The museum also owns a Catalina, of course it does, but it is currently being restored in Michigan - before it is returned for public display. Chris Zappone travelled as a guest of Alaska Airlines. He was hosted at Alohilani Resort Waikiki Beach by Hawaiʻi Tourism Oceania. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

A leader of one of the state’s major universities says the institution will “vigorously oppose” a planned merger of Curtin, Murdoch and the University of WA after the Cook government announced it will progress a business case to create a mega-university. Curtin University vice-chancellor Harlene Hayne. Premier Roger Cook and Tertiary and International Education Minister Tony Buti on Sunday announced plans to build a business case to guide the proposed merge of three of the state’s top universities before a final decision is made. According to the state government, the plan will be undertaken by the Department of the Premier and Cabinet, with input from a steering committee led by Western Australian businessman Mark Barnaba as chair and medical researcher Professor Fiona Wood as deputy chair. However, Curtin University vice chancellor Professor Harlene Hayne expressed deep concern about the merger and said the institution is planning to oppose the proposal.

Advertisement

“Curtin will vigorously oppose this in the best interests of our more than 67,000 students, 10,000 staff, 300,000 graduates and Western Australia’s economic future,” she said. “Cost, waste, and loss of choice, jobs and legacy will be the hallmarks of the planned merger of universities proposed by the Western Australian government today. “Every graduate of UWA, Curtin and Murdoch holds a degree from an institution that may not exist in the future.” Hayne said while the benefits of a potential merger have never been clearly articulated by the state government, she is also aware of the significant costs, risks and disruptions a merger would create for WA’s future. “We have been clear from the outset that Curtin does not support a forced merger,” she said.

Advertisement

“A three-way merger of Curtin, UWA and Murdoch would create a mega-university of almost 120,000 students - a scale unmatched in Australia and rare internationally. Size at that level brings complexity, not competitiveness, and draws efforts away from our core purposes of teaching, learning and student support. Related Article Exclusive

University Are WA’s universities ‘scaremongering’ over merger plans? “As WA faces a cost-of-living crisis, housing pressures, critical shortages of healthcare workers and growing pressure on hospital beds, I can’t see how spending more than a billion dollars in this way will benefit Western Australians.” Then-education minister Tony Buti commissioned a review of the state’s tertiary sector in 2023 after concerns were raised about plummeting student numbers and research grants, and WA university standings compared to their east coast counterparts. The review prompted Buti to commission a cost-benefit analysis of the three merger options mid- last year, which was led by former Labor heavyweight Alannah MacTiernan.

Advertisement

According to the state government, both studies found that merging the three WA public universities would provide maximum benefits to the WA economy and the creation of long-term jobs for Western Australians. They also found that WA is missing out on vital international and national research funding, which a strengthened university will be better positioned to win, further boosting the WA economy. Buti said the business case is a critical step towards determining the best approach to maintaining a modern, globally competitive university sector here in Western Australia for the long-term. “We have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to secure the future education of our children and future leaders and strengthen our economy by ensuring our higher education offerings remain relevant and attractive, so it is important we get this right,” he said. “Western Australia not only needs to deliver world-class education for students; we also need to build on our existing capability to deliver leading research.

Advertisement

“The business case is about doing the detailed work - confirming costs, transition arrangements, and implementation pathways ahead of a final decision being made.” Cook said ensuring local workers have the skills needed for WA’s jobs of the future is one of his government’s top priorities. “We have rebuilt our TAFE campuses and made hundreds of priority courses free for Western Australians, so we can get more local workers into local jobs,” he said. “The next opportunity to get WA workers job-ready is to ensure that we have a world-class university system that is delivering for Western Australians right across our State. “While the reports we have undertaken to date have identified the benefits of university mergers, we need to do more work on the potential costs and ability for the reforms to be funded by the universities themselves before making a final decision.”

Advertisement

WA opposition education spokesman Liam Staltari raised concerns over the cost of the proposal to the state’s taxpayers. “I think the jobs it will create are for the lawyers and consultants who will pick over a merger process for years at a time, which is exactly the concern that we have, and which would not deliver value for money for taxpayers,” he said. “We haven’t seen the review, we haven’t seen the cost-benefit analysis, and if the cost-benefit analysis doesn’t capture the cost, then actually it’s not worth the paper it’s written on.”

Hamming it up in front of more than 5000 devoted Samoa fans at Mt Druitt on Saturday, Jarome Luai was in his element. Tossing his cap into the crowd after excitedly joining his international teammates on stage, the 29-year-old was given a rapturous reception. Jarome Luai (centre) and Junior Paulo (right) will play together for Parramatta as well as Samoa. NRL Wests Tigers supporters probably don’t feel as warmly about him after his much-discussed mid-contract signing with the PNG Chiefs and eventual exit. But Luai’s new club teammate and national captain Junior Paulo has welcomed the five-eighth with open arms to Parramatta, where he will spend next season before heading to Port Moresby.

Advertisement

There is a Samoan infusion coming at the Eels, with Spencer Leniu, Jaydn Su’A and Luai joining seasoned front-rower Paulo and Ronald Volkman at their Kellyville base. Luai will only be there for a year, as Jonah Pezet was last season before linking with the Broncos, but Parramatta plan to make the most of it. Jarome Luai’s time at the Tigers did not pan out as planned. Sydney Morning Herald, Getty, NRL Images Speaking at the launch of the World Cup in Sydney, Paulo threw his support behind the four-time grand final winner, who drew headlines for flying to PNG for sponsorship appearances while at the Tigers and for missing the club’s presentation night last month. “As someone who knows him … he’s someone that is misunderstood. He’s a competitor, and I think it’s probably been a bit unfair, the treatment that he’s copped over recent weeks,” he said.

Advertisement

“He hasn’t done any wrong. It’s just one of those things where there’s always going to be someone who’s opinionated. Luckily for ‘Rome’, nothing fazes him. “There’s a reason why he’s won four comps, so that’s the experience we want to bring at Parramatta. We’re looking forward to it.” Jarome Luai at the Samoa fan day on Saturday. Instagram The addition of Leniu on a four-year deal is another plus for Parramatta coach Jason Ryles. The former Penrith forward is returning to Sydney’s west after winning a fourth premiership ring with the Roosters last Sunday. Leniu’s devastating cameo off the bench against Newcastle helped turn the match in favour of the Roosters.

Advertisement

“When you look at those guys’ resumes, there’s a lot of experience that you’re bringing into the team. Those guys know how to win,” said Paulo, who is close to agreeing to an extension with the Eels himself following a contract standoff. “Spencer has always been a firecracker … when you do it the way he did it [in the grand final] it was momentum changing for the Roosters. Luckily for us at Parra, now we get to have him on our side.” Spencer Leniu shows off his premiership ring after the grand final. Getty Images Before then, the Eels’ Samoa contingent have their eyes on the World Cup. Finalists against Australia at Old Trafford in the 2022 edition of the tournament, the quality of their squad indicates they can again contend for the cup.

Advertisement

Aside from Luai, Leniu and Paulo, the Samoa squad features superstars such as Stephen Crichton, Brian To’o and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow as well as electric Melbourne fullback Sua Fa’alogo and emerging talents such as Jermaine McEwen and Francis Manuleleua, who excelled in the Knights’ run to the grand final. Related Article Rugby League World Cup ‘Fingers crossed’: Walker hopes to secure new Roosters deal before November 1 Samoa begin their campaign with a group-stage game against France at CommBank Stadium on Friday night and are looking to make more history after their landmark appearance in the final four years ago. “We addressed it early when we got into camp that we don’t want to be the team that sort of dwells on those memories, although they were very good ones,” said Paulo. “We want to be able to build and move forward and hit the ground running in this World Cup. We want to be able to make a statement.”
