The Wallabies were taken to the hurt locker by the All Blacks on Saturday, and the methodology used against them would have been all-too-familiar. Former Wallabies coach Dave Rennie’s imprint was all over the All Blacks’ performance, so the Wallabies knew what was coming and will feel a little disappointed at how they failed to stop it. The high ball was an issue, but it’s an issue for everyone these days, and the Wallabies’ main area of improvement before the rematch in Sydney on Saturday will be to put some pressure on the ball carrier. Loading Even in the first half, players such as All Blacks No.8 Wallace Sititi were happily taking the space offered to him by the Wallabies. The All Blacks had two or three metres to wind up before they hit the advantage line and it was a factor that took a massive toll as the Test wore on. Some Wallabies jackallers will feel they didn’t get much protection from the officials when the All Blacks came in from the side, but if you can’t stop a Rennie side on the gainline they are going to keep coming to unleash a back line that has markedly improved since last year.

Advertisement

The good news for the Wallabies is that they can resolve the issue, but they’ll need to get in the faces of the All Blacks on Saturday. Suaalii’s tackle technique remains an issue Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii can’t seem to get some bad habits out of his game. His no-arms tackle on Jordie Barrett in the 69th minute was no doubt borne out of frustration, but he is developing a reputation as a dangerous tackler. It’s a shame because Suaalii’s shift to the wing is unlocking his athletic potential on attack. However, his tackle on Barrett wasn’t even close to being legal and his defensive reads will be targeted by the All Blacks. All Blacks halfback Cam Roigard puts boot to ball against the Wallabies. Getty Images Hip-drop blitz is coming to rugby

Advertisement

Rob Valetini’s tackle on Leroy Carter in the second half at Eden Park will be illegal from November 1 – and will likely result in a ban. Carter was injured in Valetini’s hip-drop tackle and there is no doubt that it can cause damage, but players will be in a race against time to change their techniques for the end-of-year tour. World Rugby issued the update on the hip-drop tackle earlier this week, and said they were relatively rare, but once you start looking for illegalities in rugby you’ll tend to find them. Smaller players, such as No.9s and No.10s, are particularly prone to using the hip-drop tackles as a way of bringing bigger opponents to the ground, so the November Tests may open up a can of worms. Related Article Australian rugby Ikitau out of Sydney Bledisloe but Valetini to avoid hip-drop scrutiny Why the high ball is so hard to defend There was a moment in the second half that summed up the Wallabies’ struggles under the high ball – All Blacks halfback Cam Roigard put up a box kick from inside his own territory and No.6 Tupou Vaa’i ran on to the ball at full speed to regather it. After escort runners were deemed to be illegal at the end of 2024, the team kicking the ball has all the rights in the high-ball contest. A few years ago, there is no way the Wallabies would have let Vaa’i run a clear line to get that box kick: he would have been shepherded out of the way. As noted in the top item, the high ball is a headache for everyone in Test rugby: even the Springboks struggled with it against the Wallabies in Perth. The rewards are coming for teams who kick well, and Wallabies halfback Ryan Lonergan was second best to Roigard on Saturday. It was uncharacteristic from Lonergan, but he was one of many Wallabies who had an off night in Auckland. Paradoxically, his sub-par performance reflected how important he has become for Les Kiss’ side. Dan Botha on the charge for the Waratahs. Getty Images

Advertisement

The Tahs prop involved in a scrum clinic It’s a long way from Sydney to Whangarei in New Zealand’s far north in more ways than one, but Waratahs prop Dan Botha looks as happy as a pig in muck. Botha played a key role in Northland’s quarter-final win against Tasman in New Zealand’s NPC on Friday, anchoring his team’s dominant scrum. Northland have used that set-piece as a weapon all season, winning penalty after penalty, so it is highly likely that Botha will return to Australia with a few new tricks up his sleeve. The Waratahs will be delighted, because Botha will now get to play in a semi-final and experience all the pressure that goes with that. The prop wasn’t first choice for a lot of the Northland campaign, but injury gave him an opportunity and he has grabbed it with both hands. He even performed in a stirring team haka before the quarter-final, so the move to New Zealand has been a rich experience for the 24-year-old.

title: Coalition defends migration cuts on economic grounds, rejects One Nation-style bans
text:
In Brief Coalition says cutting migration to 100,000 would lift productivity by prioritising higher-skilled workers.

Taylor rejected One Nation-style country bans, saying migrants should be judged on conduct and character.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has defended the Coalition's proposed migration overhaul as an economic reform designed to boost productivity, while rejecting the idea of banning migrants based on their country of origin.

The Coalition's plan would cut net overseas migration (NOM) to 100,000, about a third of current levels, while increasing the share of "high-value" migrants entering Australia.

They have called it the "biggest cut to immigration in Australian history".

However, Taylor's comments to ABC's Insiders on Sunday also appeared to mark a shift in tone from his last appearance on the show.

This time, he repeatedly framed the changes as an economic measure aimed at boosting productivity and competitiveness, rather than focusing on national security or cultural concerns.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Taylor highlights migration plan as economic reform

Taylor argued Australia's migration system should be focused on attracting workers with skills that increase productivity, rather than relying on population growth to drive economic activity.

"We are reducing the numbers and raising the standards," Taylor said.

"Because we are raising the standards, raising the incomes and tax paid of people coming into this country, that can be budget-neutral.

"It will raise productivity, it will raise competitiveness, it will raise the average income of the people coming into this city."

Taylor said the policy would increase the average skill level of migrants entering Australia while reducing overall numbers through changes to a range of visa programs, including student, graduate and bridging visas.

He repeatedly argued migration settings should be geared towards lifting productivity rather than simply increasing population growth.

"What's happening under Labor is they are driving economic growth through population growth alone," he said.

Bringing in more highly skilled migrants would put downward pressure on inflation because it would raise productivity, Taylor argued, saying "this is pretty simple economics".

The Coalition plans to dramatically cut temporary visa holders under their proposed migration policy. Source: SBS News

"When you bring someone to Australia, you are bringing demand and supply. If that person is low-skilled, you are bringing more demand than supply. If they are high-skilled, you are bringing the opposite, actually bringing more supply.

"One of the reasons why we've had a collapse in productivity in this country ... is that our immigration program has not been working to drive up our productivity and it should be."

He also defended the Coalition's proposal to halve Australia's humanitarian intake to 10,000 places, saying "charity begins at home" and such measures were designed to "balance the budget".

Taylor distances Coalition from One Nation approach

While much of Taylor's defence of the policy focused on economics, he also sought to draw a distinction between the Coalition's approach and proposals advanced by One Nation.

The comments marked a different emphasis from Taylor's previous appearance on the same program in April, when he argued migrants from "bad countries" posed a higher risk to Australia.

Pressed at the time on which countries he considered "bad", Taylor pointed to Iran and referred to security concerns involving people arriving from Gaza.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

Asked on Sunday why the Coalition had not gone as far as One Nation in proposing immigration restrictions based on nationality, Taylor rejected the comparison.

"I've always said we will discriminate not based on the country someone comes from or their race or their religion, but based on the person and whether that person is a suitable person to be a resident or citizen of this country," he said.

"That's what we should focus on, and we should judge people on their character and conduct, not the colour of their skin."

Taylor maintained that some countries could present higher risks for security agencies to assess.

"It is true that risks are higher where there is a bad regime — there is no question about that."

"That doesn't mean screen them all out. That means make sure you are assessing those risks appropriately."

One Nation has previously proposed measures targeting migration from specific countries, including pausing new migration from countries subject to a federal government 'do not travel' warning.

However, Taylor also linked the Coalition's migration policy to a broader focus on screening prospective visa holders.

"People who do not believe in our system of law, people who do not believe in our basic freedoms, they shouldn't be coming to this country," he said.

"If they've got here on a visa, they should be thrown out."

Later on Sunday, other Coalition figures reiterated those sentiments, following reports that the flydubai co-pilot accused of attempting to hijack a flight bound for Israel was allegedly radicalised while studying in Melbourne.

Opposition home affairs spokesperson Jonno Duniam said there was no place for "hate preachers who spread extremism, glorify terrorism or encourage violence".

"That is why the Coalition will tighten visa laws to keep those who preach hatred out of Australia and deport non-citizens who promote violent extremism," he said.

“At a federal level, we also need stronger visa screening, better intelligence sharing and properly resourced counter-terrorism agencies. That is why the Coalition has committed to establishing an Enhanced Screening Coordination Centre to bring together our intelligence, policing and border protection capabilities."

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Australia had its toughest-ever powers to prevent violent extremists entering the country.

"I've been using them to be able to scan and assess whether someone has a history of being a problem before we give them a visa, and we've been cancelling visas when people are here, and we've been stopping people from coming here in the first place," he told News24 on Sunday.

The economic debate over immigration levels

Taylor's argument rests on the idea that a smaller, more highly skilled migration intake would boost productivity while reducing pressure on housing and infrastructure.

However, the economic impacts of migration cuts remain heavily debated among economists, migration experts, business groups and policymakers.

Critics argue lower migration can reduce labour supply, tax and visa revenue, population growth, consumer spending and business activity, particularly in industries that rely heavily on migrant workers.

A 2021 Treasury paper estimated each skilled migrant provides a $198,000 benefit to the Australian economy because they generally arrive in the country after finishing their education.

The average Australian costs the budget $85,000 across their lifetime because they receive more money back in services than they pay in taxes.

Debate over migration's impact on housing has also intensified in recent years. While higher migration can increase demand for homes, some experts argue migrant workers are also needed to address labour shortages in the construction sector.

In September, Burke said migration cuts would inevitably come with economic trade-offs and warned no industry would be immune from their effects.

"No matter what you do, if you are lowering (immigration) numbers, there are challenges across the visa system and across the Australian economy," he told SBS News.

"I can't quarantine any sector of Australia. What I can do is make sure — as numbers are lowered, and they need to be lowered because of the challenges we have with housing supply — I want the rest of the economy to have the softest landing possible."

Labor plans to cut NOM down to 225,000 by 2028, focusing heavily on "visa hopping", international students, backpackers, and bridging visas.

One Nation plans to cap visas at 130,000 per year, which they say will ease pressure on housing, wages, and infrastructure.

title: South Melbourne stun Victory to claim Australia Cup
text:
in brief South Melbourne have won the Australia Cup for the first time.

The 1-1 final came down to a penalty shootout on Saturday night.

South Melbourne will dare to dream of an elusive A-League berth after becoming the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup by beating Melbourne Victory on penalties in an emotion-charged blockbuster final.

In one of the greatest nights in Australian domestic soccer history, former NSL powerhouses South first took Victory to extra time, then fought back from 1-0 down to level it at 1-1 at the death before winning 4-3 on penalties in front of a pumping sellout crowd of 29,911 fans at AAMI Park.

It was the biggest moment in 22 years for South, locked out of top-flight football like other NSL club when that league folded in 2024.

South, who have long craved an A-League licence, only strengthened their bid for the position with a win that capped off an extraordinary evening.

"I really cannot find any excuse not to see this club to play in the A-League," coach Sinisa Cohadzic said.

It came after he urged his players to seize their chance in their 54th game this season, after losing the OFC Pro League final to Auckland FC.

"I said to them that tonight sometimes the reality surpasses even the most beautiful dreams, and tonight was one of those nights," he said.

"It was one of those nights where they had to believe that they can get a result."

Denis Genreau scored an athletic, improvised half-volley in the 95th minute to put Victory in front, before Max Mikkola forced home an equaliser in the 117th minute to send the game to penalties and the crowd into ecstasy.

In the penalty shootout, South goalkeeper Javier Lopez was the hero and won the Mark Viduka Medal as man of the match.

Lopez initially saved former South captain Harrison Sawyer's penalty but was ruled to have come off his line - but then saved the re-take too.

"I remember in January when the club said we want to win the Australia Cup. I said 'you guys, that would be crazy'," Lopez said.

"Now we are the champions."

South scored all their penalties before Victory skipper Jason Davidson, son of South great Alan Davidson, hit his must-score spot-kick over the bar.

In becoming the first NPL team to win the Australia Cup, South have succeeded where Heidelberg last year and Sydney United 58 in 2022 could not.

With the win, South also technically claim a berth in next season's Asian Champions League 2 competition.

The defeat also extends Victory's silverware drought, with the club's most recent trophy the 2021 Australia Cup.

South certainly played up to the occasion, taking the game to Giovanni Savarese's Victory and making their mark on their biggest night in years in an incredible atmosphere.

A huge contingent of their fans packed the south end of AAMI Park, holding banners of club legends including Ange Postecoglou, Ferenc Puskas and John Margaritis.

"You guys have stuck with us for 20 years, playing in the NPL and you've shown tonight what this future holds for this great club," said captain Marco Jankovic.

The only lowlight of the night was a section of the crowd at the South end booing the Welcome to Country before the match.

Victory should have taken the lead in the 78th minute when Santos' poor shot allowed Lopez to make an extraordinary save with his knees.

But there was nothing Lopez could do in extra-time to stop himself being lobbed by Genreau's strange half-volley, which bounced over the line before he could grab it.

Then, with the clock winding down, South substitute Jordan Swibel burst down the right and sent in a ball that caused chaos and ended with Mikkola toe-poking home.

AAMI Park erupted and when the game was sent to penalties minutes later, only one club ever felt on top.

"We were not surprised by the stadium, by the environment ... it was a proper Australia Cup the way it should be," Savarese said.

"I think it will be remembered as one of the most iconic.

"Unfortunately, on our side, I wish we lifted the trophy."

title: Why we're still living with password rules their creator regrets
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Passwords are supposed to keep us safe. Instead, they can leave us jumping through hoops just to end up less protected than where we started.

For years, we've been told a "strong" password needs a capital letter, a number, and a special character. But the rules designed to make passwords harder to crack were based on logic instead of evidence. It also made them harder to remember—pushing people to reuse the same passwords or make predictable changes.

That password paradox forced a rethink of one of the internet's most familiar security rituals almost ten years ago, and even one of the people who helped popularise the rules acknowledged they didn't work.

When William "Bill" Burr was a mid-level manager at the United States' National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), he was tasked with writing guidance on electronic authentication and password security.

That advice, published in 2004, helped cement the now-familiar idea that passwords should meet complexity requirements, including minimum length and a mix of uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers, and special characters.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In 2017, Burr told The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) he regretted much of the guidance.

In the end, it was probably too complicated for a lot of folks to understand very well, and the truth is, it was barking up the wrong tree.

"It just drives people bananas," he said at the time.

When NIST updated its password guidance that same year, it moved away from some of those requirements, advising organisations against mandatory character-composition rules and routine password expiration.

Nearly a decade later, however, those rules remain common across websites and workplaces. So what does the evidence tell us about what actually makes a password secure?

The first computer passwords

The term password dates back to the late 1700s, and the idea of a secret phrase or access code to control entry goes back even further.

The first widely recognised computer password emerged in the early 1960s at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, as researchers worked on a system that let multiple people share access to a single computer.

In 1961, computer scientist Fernando Corbató led a project that developed the Compatible Time-Sharing System, or CTSS.

Fernando Corbató pioneered the use of computer passwords in the early 1960s. Source: Supplied / MIT Museum

Like a telephone exchange, the system let multiple users access a computer at the same time. But because they were sharing one machine, researchers needed a way to separate users and protect their individual files.

The password offered a simple solution: each user could have a secret string of characters controlling access to their files.

Corbató would later describe passwords as "kind of a nightmare" in a 2014 WSJ interview.

Why password complexity rules can backfire

Lorrie Cranor, a computer scientist and cybersecurity researcher at Carnegie Mellon University in Pennsylvania, tells SBS News passwords are "not a terrible idea" in a world where you have just one or two passwords.

But now we have the problem that we all have many passwords, because we have many accounts.

The premise behind password-composition rules was straightforward: if people were required to use a mix of letters, numbers and symbols, their passwords would be harder for attackers to guess.

But when those rules were first developed, evidence on how people would respond was limited.

NIST's initial guidelines also included a caveat: "Unfortunately, we do not have much data on the passwords users choose under particular rules."

It wasn't due to a lack of effort. In his 2017 interview, Burr said he even asked NIST's computer administrators to view actual passwords on their network, but they reportedly refused because of privacy concerns. The authors were therefore left to rely heavily on logic about how users might behave.

Researcher Lorrie Cranor's 'Security Blanket' features 1,000 of the most common passwords exposed in the 2009 RockYou breach. Source: Supplied / Lorrie Cranor

Since then, research has shown that the human response to password complexity is more complex.

A 2021 study from James Cook University found that increasing the number of password complexity rules did not necessarily produce stronger passwords and could increase user frustration.

It also found that users adopted strategies to make passwords easier to remember, including reusing passwords.

Why password reuse is a security problem

There are many ways to make a password weak, but reusing it across multiple services is one of the biggest risks.

Troy Hunt has seen many bad passwords. In 2013, he created Have I Been Pwned, a service that allows people to check whether their email address has appeared in a known data breach.

"As the internet came along, we already had these well-established principles that a password is memorable; it's something that you can type in," he tells SBS News.

"That came from an era where you needed things like physical presence in order to access services."

Troy Hunt (left) created Have I Been Pwned in 2013 to help people check whether their email address has been exposed in a data breach. Source: AP / Carolyn Kaster

But the internet changed the scale of the problem. People now have passwords for email, banking, shopping, social media, work systems and countless other services.

Hunt says the path of least resistance for people trying to make memorable passwords is to make them reusable.

NIST's 2017 guidance recommended checking passwords against lists of previously compromised passwords, as well as common and predictable choices, rather than relying solely on composition rules.

Shortly after, Hunt expanded his site to include a password checker.

Reused passwords are risky because once a password is exposed in a data breach, it's not only that breached service that is at risk.

Chances are it's going to be the same password that they use to buy that T-shirt or something online as they use to log onto the corporate network.

"And maybe the only thing that'll be different is the number on the end, depending on how many times they've had to rotate it," Hunt says.

NIST's current guidance recommends that organisations block commonly used, expected or compromised passwords rather than relying solely on rules about the types of characters a password contains.

What makes a good password policy?

When Carnegie Mellon University updated its password policy to include more complexity requirements, Cranor was already studying privacy and security usability.

So when her colleagues came to her complaining about the difficulty of the new requirements, she saw an opportunity.

Cranor and her team started studying password policies, hoping to answer a simple question: what is the best password policy an organisation can have?

"We wrote 20 papers and finally came up with the answer," she says.

The answer wasn't to include more special characters or numbers. Instead, the research pointed towards giving users more freedom by using an add-on to assess password strength.

The team developed an evidence-based password strength meter that assesses a password as it is created, rather than simply checking whether it meets a predetermined mix of characters.

It can also check the potential password against a list of common or exposed passwords to limit reuse.

You can put this on the web browser so that people are creating the password on the browser and are not sending the password over the internet.

"Of course, I know no organisations that are actually doing this."

Why companies still use password complexity rules

Jose-Miguel Bello Villarino is a senior research fellow at the University of Sydney Law School. He says technical standards can have misleading names.

"Technical standards are agreements in the industry among the dominant players in the way technical goods or processes are developed in the future," he tells SBS News.

"The tricky bit is that if it's something that is not legally mandated as a technical standard that has to be implemented, the people developing the things need to see a value in changing the way they're doing things."

The exception is when the change in standards relates to a safety risk.

"When it's a safety-related issue, and the standard has been adapted to these kinds of new circumstances, and you do not use that new standard, what you're risking is liability, because you are not meeting the standard," he says.

Even then, if one standards body adopts new guidelines, several different standards bodies must also update theirs for organisations to be able to make changes while remaining compliant with the relevant industry body.

Researcher Lorrie Cranor turned her bad-password fabric design into a range of dresses, including long-sleeved and formal versions, to raise awareness about password security. Source: Supplied / Lorrie Cranor

Cranor says security is about balancing risk with cost and benefit.

"There are a lot of security standards that companies follow and they're not all tied actually to the NIST guidelines," she says.

There's no perfect system, but if you're a security manager and you are appearing to be relaxing your requirements and then there's a breach, you're going to get the blame.

"Even if that's not true."

Hunt agrees. He says retaining the older rules often comes down to a "compliance officer with a checklist".

"A lot of security guidance has evolved, particularly in the last nine years since NIST put out their guidance. But a lot of computer systems and a lot of compliance regimes have taken a very long time to catch up as well."

So, what makes a strong password?

Cranor's main advice for making good passwords is not to make them yourself. Instead, she says to use a password manager to generate and store them.

You are not good at generating random passwords; your password manager is.

Hunt says the best passwords are the "ones you can't remember".

There is a small subset of passwords where this advice doesn't help, such as the password for your laptop or the one used to access your password manager.

Hunt describes this as distinguishing "what do you actually need to remember versus what do you need to be able to retrieve".

For the passwords you actually need to remember, contemporary advice generally favours length over arbitrary complexity.

One way to get that length is to use passphrases, but the key is to make the phrase hard to guess and ideally, random.

"Except the problem with random is that most of us are not very good at remembering things that actually are random," Cranor says.

"If you are, then do that. Roll a dice, pull from a hat, make something actually random."

To avoid this kind of predictability, Cranor recommends taking a memorable sentence that makes sense to you and using the first two letters of each word to create a new string, with some punctuation or a digit added somewhere in the middle.

And where its possible, Hunt suggests choosing non-password alternatives like passkeys. But their uptake has been slow, and he warns people will still have to deal with passwords for many years to come.

They will still be there because they will take a very, very long time to die.

title: Flydubai co-pilot drifted towards 'extremism and terrorism' while studying at RMIT
text:
In brief Omani national Hammam al-Hammami become acquainted with individuals from a group called "My Centre", run by a Lebanese man known as "Abu Hamza".

The co-pilot attacked captain Smit Machchhar with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month.

The Omani Flydubai co-pilot who was accused of trying to crash a plane into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport last month was radicalised at an Australian mosque while studying in Melbourne in 2017, according to the United Arab Emirates attorney general.

Omani national Hammam al-Hammami, 29, allegedly attempted to hijack flight FZ1073 with 182 people onboard travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September before passengers and crew intervened.

A statement by UAE attorney general Hamad Saif al-Shamsi shared on UAE government social media said al-Hammami's radicalisation happened when was a student at the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT). During mosque visits, al-Hammami became acquainted with individuals associated with a centre known as "My Centre".

title: Positive or problematic? Here's how much fibre you really need
text:
IN BRIEF: Fibre-maxxing has swept the algorithm, but it has multiple health benefits.

Experts say it's important fibre is consumed as food, and not supplements.

Are you getting enough fibre in your diet?

The recommended daily fibre intake is 30g for men and 25g for women, but Australian men and women consume on average about 21g and 18g of fibre per day, respectively. So, you're probably not.

Dietitians have been calling for Australians to increase their fibre intake for decades, and now the challenge has made its way to social media.

Enter the fibre-maxxer: A person committed to hitting, and even exceeding, their daily fibre target.

Online fibre-maxxers promote eating more fruits and vegetables and increasing dietary fibre intake by adding seeds, grains and vegetables to regular foods. This includes putting chia seeds in soft drinks, beans on avocado toast, grains in homemade bread, or adding a cup of legumes to rice.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Can you have too much fibre?

Program director of human nutrition and associate professor at Adelaide University, Evangeline Mantzioris, said that while fibre-maxxing was probably "one of the more positive" social media-fuelled food trends, some elements could be "problematic".

"We actually do need to increase the amount of fibre in our diet," Mantzioris told SBS News.

She said the daily intake suggestion of 25 to 30g per day was based on attaining the best health outcomes, including a reduction of colon cancer, "which is one of the most preventable diseases we have".

"But I understand some are suggesting intakes up to 50 grams a day, possibly more, and there isn't a lot of good evidence that having such extremely high levels may provide any additional benefits."

While there is no upper limit on how much fibre you can eat, more fibre means your body produces more flatulence.

"One of the biggest problems, I guess, is gas, right? No one wants to be gassy out in public."

Another issue, Mantzioris said, is fluid intake.

It was imperative to drink a healthy amount of fluids throughout the day, as without fluids, high fibre can cause constipation, rather than ease it.

"I describe it as it's a bit like trying to clean the bathroom with a dry sponge or a wet sponge. The wet sponge is going to work a lot better than the dry sponge," she said.

"Any increase in fibre will result in an increase in wind, and what we normally tell people to do is to do it slowly."

Foods like hemp seeds, quinoa, nuts, and legumes are high in dietary fibre. Source: Getty / Tanja Ivanova

Don't "go from nothing to 40 grams of fibre in one day". Instead, Mantzioris said, gradually increase high-fibre foods in your diet. This will also help ensure it is a "sustainable" transition for your gut microbiome, the complex community of trillions of microorganisms that live in your digestive tract.

"We know that the bacteria in our gut use that fibre for their survival, and we know that the fibre that comes from whole foods like fruit, vegetables, legumes, beans, nuts, and seeds gives you the healthiest type of microbiome possible", as opposed to the bacteria that thrive on "sometimes foods", which are unhealthy for your body.

"So it's sort of like this lovely symbiotic relationship between your bacteria and you, and the more healthy food you give them, the better off they are, and the better off you are."

Why fibre should come from food

"It's all about balance," Mantzioris said, stressing that fibre intake should come from food, not supplements, which she said some fibremaxxing influencers might be recommending.

"By using supplements, you're missing out on all of the additional nutrients that are in the foods that they originally come from."

She said the best way to avoid "overdosing" on fibre would be to get it from food.

"And get it from a range of different foods — there are a lot of different types of fibres, and they each play a different role in our bodies."

"It's important to eat beans, to eat fruit, eat vegetables, and to eat cereals, to get the maximum benefits from all the different types of fibres, as well as the nutrients that come with all those foods that we know promote health," she said.

What is fibre?

Fibre is a nutrient found in many foods that reduces your risk of chronic disease and keeps your digestive system healthy.

Adequate dietary fibre is essential for proper gut function. It has also been related to risk reduction for some chronic diseases, including heart disease, certain cancers and diabetes.

There are three kinds of fibre: soluble fibre, which slows down digestion, like oats and barley; insoluble fibre, like whole grains, which bulks your stool and speeds up the movement of food through your digestive tract; and resistant starch, found in boiled and cooled potatoes, which ferments in your gut and acts as a prebiotic to feed beneficial bacteria.

Mantzioris said there were "a few reasons" why fibre intake was so consistently low in Australia.

Only about 5 per cent of Australians are meeting the minimum requirements for vegetables in their diet, at 5 serves a day.

Chia seeds, native to Central America, are popular amongst online fibremaxxers due to their exceptionally high fibre content Source: Getty / Stefania Pelfini la Waziya

"And of course, fibre vegetables are a great source of fibre," Mantzioris said.

She pointed to the ever-increasing popularity of high-protein diets, or "the protein craze".

"When you're consuming more of one food, you're dropping out another essential food group, which is providing you with essential nutrients."

"They're focusing on their protein intake, and we know that roughly 98 per cent of Australians meet their protein requirement".

Beans, she said, were a great example of a high-protein food with multiple benefits.

"The benefit of that protein source is that it also gives you the fibre, and all the antioxidants that we need to fight disease, to reduce oxidative stress in the body and reduce inflammation."

"Every different colour you have in the plant foods represents a different nutrient that's useful for the body."

Finally, she said, "There's an aversion to carbohydrates in our society."

"People see carbohydrates as the problem food when it comes to trying to manage their weight — and all of the carbohydrate-rich foods also provide us with a lot of fibre."

title: Two goals but no win for Matildas in Germany friendly
text:
in brief Australia lost 4-2 in an away game against Germany.

The match was an international friendly ahead of next year's FIFA Women's World Cup.

The Matildas may count the cost of an error-riddled 4-2 defeat to an understrength Germany after star striker Sam Kerr emerged from the game complaining of ankle soreness.

With limited international windows remaining before next year's FIFA Women's World Cup in Brazil, Friday's (Saturday AEDT) clash against the world No.3 in Karlsruhe was crucial.

Headlines before the game were dominated by the absence of Manchester City star Mary Fowler (personal reasons), and she was missed as the Germans scored the opening two goals.

But captain Kerr's header on the stroke of halftime helped the visitors close the deficit before the home team's Camilla Kuver scored in the 83rd minute.

Striker Holly McNamara did find a late consolation goal for the Matildas, but Chelsea midfielder Sjoeke Nusken dashed any hopes of a draw.

Most concerningly, Kerr was taken off in the 64th minute after her ankle was trodden on minutes before her goal.

The skipper played down the severity of the injury, but added that she wasn't comfortable.

"I came in with a bit of a sore ankle," Kerr told Paramount +.

"I always plan to come off around the 60th, 70th minute. So nothing about the ankle (contributed to) coming off, but it's pretty sore now."

For Germany, the victory came despite the two-time world champions missing a plethora of stars, including captain Giulia Gwinn (ankle) and Liverpool forward Vivien Endemann (calf).

Australia will rue the missed opportunity to capitalise on their opponents' absences as a win would have helped them remain firmly in pot two out of four for the World Cup draw, meaning a mathematically better chance for a more favourable draw.

"The biggest thing for us is we have to make sure that any time we retrieve the ball or we have situations where we have the opportunity to win the ball, we have to keep it better," coach Joe Montemurro said.

"We probably created a lot of chances for Germany, with a lot of our technical errors which we know now that we can't get away with at this top level."

Despite the result, the Matildas will have something to celebrate as defender Tori Tumeth made her debut off the bench in the second half.

World No.15 Australia sent an early warning shot when Ellie Carpenter put in a dangerous cross to Kerr, but Germany upped the ante afterwards.

Defender Carlotta Wamser lofted a cross to Franziska Kett, and she used her head to guide the ball onto the feet of forward Melissa Kossler.

Seven minutes later Kossler stormed down the field and thumped the ball into the bottom left corner.

But in the dying moments of the first half, Carpenter fired a cross onto the head of Kerr and the striker closed the deficit to 2-1 at the break.

Midfielder Clare Wheeler had an opportunity go begging in the 56th minute when her shot rattled onto the crossbar.

Bayern Munich's Linda Dallmann dispatched a corner for a header by defender Kuver, and she nodded the ball past Mackenzie Arnold.

In injury time, Caitlin Foord poked the ball to McNamara, and she scored. However, Nusken whacked the ball into the bottom right corner to seal the victory.

"We can be satisfied," Kossler said.

"We set ourselves some tactical goals, wanted to try something out, and were able to implement them successfully for the most part."

title: Want the highest possible savings rate? You might find there’s a catch
text:
When the Reserve Bank lifts interest rates, borrowers pay more through higher mortgage rates and repayments, but savers benefit too.

This week, research from Canstar showed the highest ongoing savings rate hit 6 per cent, a level it says hasn't been seen in Australia in well over a decade.

The catch, however, is that you generally need to be young to qualify.

But how young?

One bank, for example, offers that rate to those under 25, while another offers it only to those aged 14 to 35.

Both, however, require monthly terms and conditions to be met, such as regular deposits, withdrawal limits, and topping out at a certain savings level.

For everyone else, some new customers are targeted with introductory offers at a high rate that apply only for a few months, while others require a high balance.

Still, for professional sharemarket investors, higher interest rates more broadly offer a challenge for them.

"We’re competing with having money in the bank," Dianne Colledge, a private client adviser at Morgans told the SBS On the Money Podcast.

"We need to be able to, as investors, generate a higher return [in] both income and growth, to compete with that and the risk of investing."

The Australian sharemarket is actually down around a quarter of a per cent so far this year, but that doesn’t take into consideration dividends.

Are falling home values able to hit a floor?

With property prices easing in most capital cities, and auction clearance rates at the lowest since July, I was really curious to see what management at REA Group had to say about housing at its annual general meeting this week.

Annual general meetings (AGMs) are held every year by listed companies to give shareholders an opportunity to meet management, discuss their concerns and listen to any market updates.

Cameron McIntyre, CEO of REA Group, which owns property website realestate.com.au, offered some hope that price falls may end soon.

That's good news if you’re an owner, but not necessarily if you’re looking to buy.

"Resilient employment, limited forced selling and homeowner equity buffers, along with ongoing constrained supply should put a floor under the falls we see," McIntyre told shareholders.

"As interest rates stabilise in the coming months, we expect consumer confidence to improve, and buyer activity to pick up."

The problem is, there’s still a risk of another interest rate rise in November, which money markets currently predict hasa near 30 per cent chance of happening.

"Interest rates are the biggest factor contributing to market uncertainty at the moment," McIntyre added at the AGM.

The company said listing volumes on its website have been driven by Melbourne and Sydney so far this financial year, but it’s started to see Brisbane, Perth and Adelaide outperform.

Telstra and the Commonwealth Bank hold their AGMs next week.

Ombudsman wants social media complaints oversight

If you've had an issue with your mobile or internet service provider and can’t resolve it with them, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman (TIO) can help.

Last week, it unveiled its 2025-26 annual report, saying it received 53,834 complaints, down 6.5 per cent from the previous year, most relating to telcos taking too long or failing to act.

Sometimes, those issues can cause financial loss, and the TIO saw a 60.7 per cent increase in people seeking compensation for disruptions and services that didn't work as expected.

The Ombudsman can order telcos to compensate consumers and small businesses for claims of up to $100,000.

But now it also wants oversight of digital services and social media.

TIO Cynthia Gebert told the SBS On the Money Podcast, when something goes wrong online, people, small businesses and community groups have no redress when big tech companies can’t or won’t resolve their issues.

“We’re calling on the government to change our jurisdiction and our remit to require digital platforms to be a member of the TIO so that consumers have somewhere free, fair and independent to go to get things sorted when things do go wrong online.”

Last financial year, 1,124 people, up 70 per cent, came to the TIO for help with their digital platform problems.

title: Australia's house prices are falling. But will that make homes more affordable?
text:
Australia's housing downturn is gathering pace, with prices now more than 5 per cent below their peak and forecasts pointing to further falls.

While that may seem like good news for first homebuyers, higher interest rates have done little to improve housing affordability so far. Four rate hikes this year have cut borrowing capacity by about 9 per cent, or $90,000, for a median-income household, according to data analytics company Cotality.

Homeowners and renters are also under pressure. According to Roy Morgan research, more than 32 per cent of borrowers are now at risk of mortgage stress — up 8.4 percentage points since January — while the rental market remains tight.

The major banks and analysts are predicting a decline of between 7 and 15 per cent, while United States investment bank Morgan Stanley has forecast the biggest price correction in 40 years.

The broader economic backdrop is also weighing on households. Interest rates are at their highest level in 15 years, while the cost of living crisis and growing fears of recession have kept consumer confidence near historic lows.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But looking across the Tasman to New Zealand and across the Pacific to Canada could provide insight into what lies ahead for Australia's property market.

All three countries have experienced housing crises, marked by unprecedented price booms during the COVID-19 pandemic, housing shortages and affordability pressures.

Since then, Australia has taken a different path. While home values in New Zealand and Canada began falling several years ago, Australia's downturn is only just beginning.

Source: SBS News

As of the first quarter of 2026, house prices relative–to–incomes had fallen substantially from their COVID-era peak in New Zealand and Canada, while Australia's remained above its pandemic-era high, according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data.

Could Australia follow a similar trajectory? And what lessons can be learned from their housing corrections?

New Zealand's housing correction

Across the ditch, average property prices rose 85 per cent between 2010 and 2020, then surged another 44 per cent during the pandemic, peaking at NZ$1.06 million ($1 million) in 2022.

Nick Goodall, head of research at Cotality New Zealand, says the property boom was fuelled by ultra-low interest rates, pandemic support measures and looser lending rules.

He describes the peak as "very artificial", with the market reversing once interest rates started to rise.

To curb post-pandemic inflation, the Reserve Bank of New Zealand lifted its cash rate 12 times in a row to 5.5 per cent by May 2023.

By comparison, Australia's cash rate peaked at 4.35 per cent in November 2023.

New Zealand then entered recession in 2023, as higher interest rates weighed on demand and the labour market weakened, contributing to about an 18 per cent decline in property values from their peak over 18 months.

Nick Goodall of Cotality New Zealand says New Zealand's property boom was driven by ultra-low interest rates, pandemic support measures and looser lending rules. Source: Supplied

Prices have remained broadly flat since.

But affordability has begun improving as interest rates have fallen, following nine consecutive rate cuts from mid-2024.

Cotality data shows the national value-to-income ratio, which measures how many years of household income are needed to buy a median-priced home, fell from a peak of 9.8 in late 2021 to 6.7 in the second quarter of 2026.

Goodall says a more useful measure is the median gross household income needed to service a mortgage, with now sits at 40 per cent, down from a peak of above 50 per cent in late 2021 and below the long-term average of 42 per cent.

Supply and planning reforms have also played a role, particularly in Auckland, where changes allowed greater housing density.

"Enabling more properties to be built on the same area of land that was available previously for only one property, certainly has led to less growth or maybe a greater decline [in prices]," Goodall tells SBS News.

Housing affordability has improved in New Zealand in recent years. Source: Getty / Hagen Hopkins

First homebuyers accounted for 29 per cent of sales in the most recent quarter, the highest proportion since Cotality started tracking the data in 2003.

Rental affordability has also improved, with rents 1.8 per cent lower in 2025 than a year earlier — the first annual decline in a decade, according to Realestate.co.nz.

[Renters have] got less competition out there, so they can take their time. They know they've got the power in their hands because there's high supply.

Meanwhile, investors have been squeezed by higher ownership costs, weaker expectations of capital gains, and softer rental returns as housing supply increased and population growth slowed.

"[Property investors] can make it work, but it's definitely not the easy game it used to be when interest rates were really low," Goodall says.

Canada's housing correction

In Canada, home prices surged more than 50 per cent during the COVID-19 pandemic, before falling about 20 per cent from their early-2022 peak.

The boom was fuelled by very low interest rates and a shift towards larger suburban homes as lockdowns and remote work changed where people wanted to live.

The Bank of Canada lifted the cash rate from 0.25 per cent in March 2022 to 5 per cent in July 2023, with prices starting to fall sharply later that year before declining more gradually.

Robert Hogue, assistant chief economist at the Royal Bank of Canada , says while the correction offered some relief, prices remained far higher than before the pandemic and housing remained particularly unaffordable in cities such as Toronto and Vancouver.

Housing affordability remains a major issue in Canadian cities such as Toronto. Source: Getty / Francois Nel

"If you ask ordinary Canadians, it's still unaffordable in many parts of Canada … it's just that it's less unaffordable than it was just a couple years ago," he tells SBS News.

He says Canada's cash rate, which has been at 2.25 per cent since October last year, which he expected to rise in the year ahead, while slower economic growth could weigh on wage growth, meaning affordability is unlikely to improve anytime soon.

A surge in post-pandemic migration added significantly to housing demand, with Canada adding more than 1.2 million people through permanent and temporary migration in 2023 alone.

The Canadian government subsequently moved to reduce migration pressure, cutting temporary resident arrivals by about 43 per cent.

It also aimed to slash permanent migration from a previous target of 500,000 to 395,000 last year, with further reductions in the years to follow.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

Hogue says curbing temporary immigration had cooled the rental market.

Data from rentals.ca this month show asking rents across Canada were down 4.2 per cent year-over-year, marking the 24th consecutive month of decline.

But Hogue says the drop in demand had a spillover effect, with condo developers launching fewer projects because of lower returns and higher building costs.

He says that could be a problem when migration picks up again.

"This is a big concern for those like me thinking ahead in three or four-or five-years' time."

What Australia can learn

New Zealand has seen housing affordability improve, while Canada continues to face significant affordability pressures.

To understand what that means for Australia, it's worth first examining why its housing market took a different path from Canada and New Zealand.

Australia's pandemic housing boom was less pronounced than those of New Zealand and Canada, with prices rising about 25 per cent between April 2020 and February 2022, according to Cotality.

After an initial fall, however, Australian property prices recovered and continued rising until reaching a new peak in March 2026. They have since fallen for six consecutive months, leaving prices 5.2 per cent below their peak.

Despite the decline, housing affordability has reached a record low on realestate.com.au's measure, with a typical-income household able to afford just 12 per cent of homes across Australia.

Independent economist Saul Eslake says Australia's downturn is only beginning this year partly because governments have until recently supported the housing market through cash grants and other schemes.

He points out Canada and New Zealand did not intervene in the same way.

Source: SBS News

Eslake also notes Australia's unemployment rate, currently 4.6 per cent, is lower than Canada's 6.4 per cent and New Zealand's 5.6 per cent, reducing pressure on households to sell and, in turn, on property prices.

While Australia's cash rate of 4.6 per cent is currently higher than New Zealand's 2.75 per cent and Canada's 2.25 per cent, Eslake notes that differences in cash rates do not necessarily translate into an equivalent difference in mortgage rates.

Canadian mortgages are often fixed for five years, with many rates until recently higher than Australian variable mortgage rates. New Zealand floating variable rates have also often sat around Australian rates, despite the country have a lower cash rate.

Eslake points out New Zealand's population growth had been slower than Australia's, partly because many New Zealanders moved across the Tasman in search of better economic opportunities, while Canada introduced measures to curb temporary migration several years ago.

Net overseas migration (NOM) looks at how many longer-term migrants are arriving in Australia each year. Source: SBS News

The federal government only announced tightened temporary migration rules last month, while the Coalition and One Nation have promised deeper cuts.

"Cuts in the immigration intake, depending on how large they are, and depending on what categories of migrants they fall on, could reduce the demand for housing," Eslake says.

Eslake estimates a 10 to 15 per cent decline in house prices over two years could improve affordability, while warning a sharper fall would harm the economy.

But for affordability to become the priority, he says there needs to be a fundamental shift in how housing is treated.

Australians have increasingly come to think about housing as a vehicle for, to use the common politician's phrase that I hate, ‘a means of getting ahead', without, of course, ever asking the question ahead of whom?

"To which the answer is your own children and grandchildren. In other words, we've come to think of housing as a vehicle for wealth accumulation, rather than a vehicle for providing basic human needs."

Even now, Eslake says governments have been reluctant to frame policy, such as changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax which have cooled investor demand, as an effort to make housing more affordable.

Economist Saul Eslake says the government has been unwilling to frame policy changes as an effort to make housing more affordable. Source: AAP / Mick Tsikas

"We have consciously sought to reduce investor demand for established housing, in order to make housing cheaper for first-home buyers, in other words, to make housing more affordable," Eslake says.

"But they haven't said that. They have run away from it … they are still captured by the idea that the main purpose of housing is a vehicle for accumulating wealth rather than meeting basic human needs."

New Zealand economist Shamubeel Eaqub argues that changing this mindset may be just as difficult as changing housing policy.

New Zealand's experience, he says, has shown that people can become so accustomed to rising house prices that accepting a different path becomes a major psychological barrier.

"When house prices are rising, I think it's very easy to kind of focus on the fact that we're just wealthier and it's just easy," he tells SBS News.

But the real work of an economy is actually much harder in terms of how we create good businesses, good jobs, good quality of life, and those wider competitive and policy settings that are good for society.

title: They booked a cheap cruise package. Then the tickets vanished
text:
When Brisbane resident Harry Harding found a sold-out cruise deal online, he was sceptical.

The eight-night Carnival Cruise sailing from Brisbane to Vanuatu and other Pacific destinations had already sold out in the cabin category he and his housemate wanted.

Then they came across an advertisement on RedNote, a Chinese social media platform, claiming cabins were still available.

Harding spent time checking the seller before handing over any money.

"There were lots of comments on the RedNote account saying the service was good and reliable, so we trusted them," he told SBS Chinese.

After paying a 10 per cent deposit, the pair received what appeared to be legitimate tickets. Confident the booking was genuine, Harding's housemate transferred the remaining balance — about US$2,500, or more than $3,500.

The booking appeared on Carnival's website. Their names were attached to it. They could log in, buy Wi-Fi packages and reserve restaurants.

"It just seemed legitimate," he said.

Then, less than a week before they were due to leave, everything disappeared.

READ MORE Think you can spot scam red flags? The warning signs are changing

"About six days before we were due to leave, we noticed the booking was gone," he said.

"From that point, they largely stopped responding to us and would just say things like, 'Please be patient'."

When Harding contacted Carnival, he says he was unable to get answers because the booking had been made using someone else's payment details.

"Because the travel agent had booked the tickets with a different credit card, the person on the hotline wouldn't give me any information for privacy reasons," he said.

Harry did his due diligence on this travel agent. But he was still scammed on a pricey Carnival Cruise holiday. Source: Supplied / SBS Chinese

"So even though it was our names and our passport numbers on the tickets, we couldn't actually do anything through Carnival."

The situation became even more complicated because the travel agent was based overseas.

"The travel agency was a Chinese travel agent and they booked the tickets through the American office of Carnival," he said.

"We're in Australia, so basically had no recourse because nobody here in Australia could help us."

Lured in by big discounts

Brisbane resident Lucy Liu says she had a similar experience.

She and three other passengers booked a five-day cruise after finding what appeared to be a heavily discounted fare through a Chinese travel agent.

The cabin was advertised for about $1,300, compared with around $1,800 on the cruise line's website.

"It was around a 30 per cent discount," Liu told SBS Chinese.

"They told us it was a last-minute promotional price, and that was what attracted us."

Like Harding, Liu believed the business appeared legitimate.

Lucy thought she was buying tickets on a cruise from a reputable seller. She later discovered Beijing authorities had revoked the company's business licence. Source: Supplied / SBS Chinese

The RedNote account carried platform verification and displayed a business licence and company name.

"They had also displayed their business licence and company name on the account," she said.

But shortly before departure, Liu learned the booking had been cancelled.

When she sought an explanation, she received conflicting answers.

"At first they blamed us, saying we had entered our information incorrectly and that the cruise company couldn't contact us, which was why the booking was cancelled," she said.

"Then someone else said it was cancelled because we hadn't checked in."

According to Liu, the cruise line advised that the payment had been reversed and the money returned to the original account used to make the booking.

Liu says she later discovered information online showing the travel company's licence had reportedly been revoked by authorities in Beijing.

Both Lucy and Harry were targeted by what appeared to be a "sophisticated" travel scam after they tried to purchase cheaper tickets for a Carnival Cruise. Source: Getty / South Florida Sun-Sentinel/TNS

"The biggest difficulty, in my view, is probably related to cross-border consumer protection," she said.

"We weren't really sure which authority we should approach to resolve the issue."

How does this happen?

Melbourne-based cruise travel agent Snow Yu, who has worked in the industry for 14 years, says heavily discounted cruise fares can be a warning sign.

"They use very low advertised prices as a hook," she told SBS Chinese.

Yu says scammers have previously focused on highly sought-after Disney cruises before shifting their attention to brands including Royal Caribbean and Carnival.

She believes cases like these may involve fraudulent payment methods.

"It could be the result of credit card fraud," she said.

"After the cardholder discovers the transaction, they may report the card or transaction to the bank and recover the money."

"Once that payment is recovered, the cruise company has to cancel the booking.

"The problem isn't necessarily the booking itself, but the method of payment."

Carnival Cruise Line told SBS Chinese that travel scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated.

"Unfortunately, travel scams are becoming increasingly sophisticated, and we urge guests to exercise caution when purchasing a holiday through third parties," a spokesperson said.

"Guests should only book directly through Carnival Cruise Line or through reputable, accredited travel agents."

Melbourne commercial lawyer Tina Ji says consumers should be cautious if they're asked to transfer money directly or make advance payments outside established booking systems.

"Potential warning signs include requests for advance payment or requests to make private/direct transfers," she said.

Ji said people involved in disputes through platforms such as WeChat or RedNote should first consider reporting the matter through those platforms, noting that cross-border cases can raise jurisdictional challenges.

Yu recommends checking industry bodies such as the Australian Travel Industry Association and Cruise Lines International Association to help verify whether a travel agent is legitimate.

'Believe the official website'

Harding and his housemate eventually recovered their money after publicly challenging the travel agent online.

He says affected customers began comparing notes and found what appeared to be links between multiple accounts advertising cruise deals under different names.

"We knew that whoever was doing this was repeating the scam just under a different name," he said.

The business would repeat the scam under different names, Harry and other consumers found. Source: Supplied / SBS Chinese

Harding posted comments warning other consumers and uploaded a video naming the travel agency.

"But in the end, because of all the pressure that we were placing on them, they did eventually refund us on the condition that we would remove the posts," he said.

"As of this day, I have not removed my post."

His advice to other travellers is simple.

"If somebody is offering you a ticket to something and it says it's sold out on the official website, believe the official website," he said.

"Don't believe the person who's trying to sell you something."

SBS Chinese contacted the travel agency involved for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.

title: The 65-year-old Greek club taking on A-League giants in sold-out Australia Cup final
text:
IN BRIEF: The South Melbourne Hellas will face Melbourne Victory this weekend in a colossal Australia Cup final.

Each team has their own storied history and represent 'old' and 'new' football in Australia.

It's a sold-out football final 12 years in the making, but with roots that go back decades, as South Melbourne take on Melbourne Victory.

The first all-Victorian Australia Cup final of the modern era will bring together two giants of Australian football representing different generations.

At Melbourne's Rectangular Stadium, four-time A-League champions Melbourne Victory will face the South Melbourne Hellas — four-time National Soccer League champions and the third non-A-League team to make an Australia Cup final.

South Melbourne, a 65-year-old club founded by Greeks, boasts former Socceroos coach Ange Postecoglou and one of football's best ever players Ferenc Puskás as alumni.

The team got here largely thanks to 25-year-old striker Bul Juach, who proved the hero in last month's semi-final, coming off the bench to score a second-half hat-trick in the 3-1 win over Queensland Lions.

Bul, nicknamed the 'Raging Bul' told SBS News, "It's a good feeling. It's massive for the club. You can see the morale, and everyone is happy."

"The boys have been welcoming. The club has been welcoming ... I just have to keep going well, and hopefully we can win some trophies."

At 12, the South Sudanese Australian migrated to Canberra, where he began playing organised sport.

"Before that it was street football," he said.

Juach said that football helped him through the adjustment of migrating to Australia, including learning the language and the culture.

"It was a big change coming from Africa, but football helped me a lot," he said.

"It's the world game — it's for everyone. That is the beauty of it."

The winner will claim silverware and a berth in next year's Asian Champions League 2, whilst South Melbourne are hoping a win will boost their cause as they seek inclusion to the A-League.

A multicultural legacy

Juach said it was "good to see" multiculturalism in the South Melbourne club.

"That is what all of Australia is about," he said.

"We are all proud to be representing this club. We can see how big it is and the ambition of the club, and we all want to be part of that."

Founded by Greek immigrants in 1959, the South Melbourne club amalgamated three clubs: South Melbourne United, Hellenic and Yarra Park.

Behind the merger was Theo Marmaras, along with Georgios Samaras, the grandfather of the former Celtic and Greece striker of the same name.

Despite the club's rich Greek diaspora connection, history and influence, Juach is today part of a diverse playing group — reflecting the sport's multiculturalism at a national level.

Ask about Socceroos of African heritage, Juach said players such as Awer Mabil, Thomas Deng, Nestory Irankunda and Mohamed Toure were an inspiration to the African community.

"Big pride. It’s all good to push the younger generation to aim for bigger things and play at these levels and stages," he said.

Two football giants of different generations

Originally called the FFA Cup, the fixture was launched in 2014 and is now known as the Australia Cup.

This season's campaign involved 777 clubs from across Australia.

Melbourne Victory has previously lifted the trophy in this competition in 2015 and 2021, both at Melbourne Rectangular Stadium, and finished runners-up to Macarthur FC at the same venue in 2024.

The A-League giants go into this final without marquee Spanish player Juan Mata, who has left the club, and under new Venezuelan coach Giovanni Savarese, appointed in June this year.

In a statement, Football Australia chief executive officer Martin Kugeler said, "Both clubs have proud histories and passionate supporter bases."

The governing body's executive director of football, Heather Garriock, said the tournament has "meant a lot to the NPL and community clubs across the country".

South Melbourne represents the traditional NPL system and a club history stretching decades, while Melbourne Victory represents the professional A-League, which started in 2005, a year after the NSL folded.

A-League entities such as Melbourne Victory, Adelaide United and Sydney FC built their own modern history. Meanwhile, legacy clubs such as South Melbourne, Heidelberg, Sydney Olympic and Marconi were relegated to state leagues, demanding a return to the national spotlight ever since.

South Melbourne captain Marco Jankovic said he was looking forward to the "special day".

title: How the ATO found itself embroiled in a battle over credit cards that forced a rethink
text:
Key Points A ban on credit card payments for tax bills has been pushed back to June 2027.

This change is one of three shifts made in October to how money moves.

The federal government has been forced to delay the Australian Taxation Office's (ATO) planned ban on the use of credit cards to pay tax bills until June 2027, following a backlash from business groups.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers announced additional funding for the ATO on Friday to maintain the payment option until at least June 2027.

The move came after critics argued the ban puts pressure on small businesses that rely on credit cards to manage cash flow.

The decision to delay was an unintended consequence of the government's broader payments reforms, which included a ban on card surcharges and lower transaction fees.

Here's how the controversy unfolded.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What has changed?

The ATO's move is linked to a broader shake-up of Australia's payments system that took effect this month.

First card surcharges were banned. Second, the rate banks charge businesses to transfer money from customers to businesses was cut from 0.8 per cent to 0.3 per cent. Thirdly, EFTPOS, Mastercard and Visa must publish the merchant fees they charge so businesses can compare rates and avoid paying higher-than-average fees.

The fourth change flows from the lower fees banks charge on transactions because they subsidise frequent flyer and rewards points programs. Banks started raising annual fees and offering fewer perks ahead of the rate changes.

Why did the ATO make the change?

The decision followed the Reserve Bank's ban on surcharges for EFTPOS, Visa and Mastercard payments, which began on 1 October. The ATO said continuing to accept credit cards and absorbing the processing fees would cost about $200 million annually.

The ATO "explored options" including with credit card companies to seek lower fees, but they did not offer fees low enough to allow the ATO to afford to continue to accept credit card payments.

Other government departments, including Border Force and the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade, say they will continue to accept credit card payments.

The ATO has said it will continue to consult with "relevant stakeholders and stewardship groups to understand how best to support those experiencing financial hardship and identify alternative arrangements for businesses and individuals who are unable to pay via other methods."

Why were people angry?

Some small businesses use credit cards to bridge or extend the gap between when a tax bill is due and having to pay it. Losing this option means finding cash sooner or arranging alternative finance. Credit cards can offer rewards such as frequent flyer points when they are used.

Business groups said there was a double standard because they have to accept cards and absorb the fees or raise prices, while the tax office simply withdrew the option to pay by card entirely. They also say the consultation period was too rushed, with just two months to adapt and raise concerns.

Why is it political?

Labor promoted the surcharge ban as a cost of living relief, but the ATO's response caused a small business backlash and the government's response was contradictory.

Ministers Anne Aly and Clare O’Neil urged further engagement and said a workable solution must be found for small businesses because they had "real concerns" about the ATO's move before the extended deadline.

Meanwhile, the Coalition pushed for the ban to be reversed. Opposition leader Angus Taylor said the government should force the ATO to reverse the decision on Friday, before the treasurer did so.

READ MORE Card surcharges are banned. Now Aussies are fuming over another charge

Opposition treasury spokesperson Tim Wilson, speaking on Friday before the backflip, said, the ATO "needs to overturn its ban because this is a situation of complete inconsistency between the standard set for small business and the standard set for the Australian Taxation Office imposed by the Albanese government".

How many people are affected?

The latest ATO data shows about 2.3 per cent of tax payments were made with credit cards in the 2024/25 financial year, most of them coming from privately owned wealthy groups, and public and multinational businesses.

The Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief Andrew McKellar said the sector was worried and angry.

"There's 4.9 million small businesses out there — active small businesses. Even if this only affects ... around 5 per cent of all of those businesses, that's a quarter of a million individual small businesses who are directly inconvenienced by this," he said.

What happens now?

Treasurer Jim Chalmers announced extra funding for the ATO to delay the credit card ban until June 2027.

"We will continue to work closely with small businesses and the ATO on this issue to get the best outcome," Chalmers said.
