title: The $10 pint is extinct – this is what you can expect to pay for a beer in every capital city
text:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

If you’ve ever done a double-take at the cost of buying a round of beers for your mates at the pub these days, your complaints have been justified: since January 2020, the average price of a pint of beer has risen by nearly $1 every 18 months, or from $9.96 to $13.76 across the nation. And if you’re in Melbourne, tough luck; you’re typically paying more than the rest of the country for Australia’s favourite beers, according to exclusive data provided by Square. Click on the interactive below to see how prices compare for your beer of choice across capital cities. Some pricing information is missing due to insufficient data in some cities, including Carlton Dry and Carlton Draught in Brisbane, and Carlton Draught and Balter XPA in Adelaide. City-level pint comparison data for VB, Asahi, Furphy and Heaps Normal was incomplete and has been excluded from the final data set. A pint of Balter XPA costs more in Melbourne ($15.70) than any other Australian city on average. The same goes for Guinness ($15.51), Carlton Draught ($13.91), Carlton Dry ($12.86) and Great Northern Super Crisp ($12.95). Meanwhile, the opposite is true for those who live in Perth, which is generally the cheapest capital city to buy a pint of those beers. “That to me suggests [those beers are] trying to do some sort of targeted discounting or trying to break in to the Western Australia market,” said beer expert and The Crafty Pint founder James Smith. “WA as a whole, in terms of hospitality and the beer production industry, has generally held firm longer than other states did.”

Advertisement

Related Article Alcohol Think Gen Z is to blame for alcohol’s decline? Think again The steepest increases came after pandemic lockdowns ended in 2022, after which most pint prices rose by about 10 per cent, said Square executive David Schnabl. “Most [pubs] held prices for as long as they could, which is why pub beer may have felt like it lagged the grocery aisle in the early inflation years,” he said. “Increases have moderated every year since, but they’ve never reversed.” The national average price of premium beers Balter XPA ($14.53) and Guinness ($14.48) have been drifting towards the $15 mark. “Craft beer was already trading at a premium, but the gap between premium and mainstream has continued to widen. The $10 pint is effectively extinct in this dataset,” said Schnabl. “Even XXXX Gold, the cheapest pint of any beer we tracked, now averages $11.24 nationally.” The Balter XPA (extra pale ale) gained popularity for being an approachable craft beer. Beer breakdown

Advertisement

Stone & Wood Pacific Ale tends to be the most consistently priced across the country, with less than $1 difference between the cheapest and most expensive city, Sydney ($14.25) and Adelaide ($15.23). Residents of Adelaide, where Coopers Brewery originated, are paying more than others to drink a Coopers Pale Ale at $13.81 (with the exception of Perth). A pint of Great Northern ($11.73), Australia’s best-selling beer, has risen more than any other major tap beer, at 43 per cent since 2020, when it was $8.21. Guinness (which has enjoyed a cultural resurgence thanks to the viral trend of “splitting the G”) is not far behind, increasing 41 per cent from $10.25 to $14.48 a pint. What’s the most you’ve paid for a pint in Australia? Let us know in the comments. Publicans in Victoria are grappling with more levies and taxes than those in some other states, including the mental health wellbeing levy and the COVID-19 debt repayment payroll tax, which impact venues where payroll exceeds $10 million. Meanwhile, higher land tax and council rates as well as stricter licensing conditions, which include a mandatory guard-to-patron ratio for late night venues, have also pushed up overheads and squeezed margins. “I certainly hear my mates who’ve got pubs say: ‘They’re f---ing killing us here,’” said Smith. But the popularity of Carlton Draught as the state’s most ordered tap beer endures.

Advertisement

Pros: delicious. Cons: increasingly expensive. iStock “I reckon there could be an element in Victoria or in Melbourne, people knowing we can charge more because people are going to buy it anyway. They might walk away from the bar and go, ‘I can’t believe how much it’s cost me for a round’, but they’re never going to look at anything else on tap.” Related Article Beer and cider From ‘splitting the G’ to the perfect pour: Eight things you need to know about Guinness Perth’s prices also appear cheaper as there’s a more “entrenched pint culture” on the west coast than the east coast, according to Titanium Property food and retail planning expert Taylor Westlake. About 8 per cent of greater Perth’s population was born in England, where pints are the standard beer size (570ml), compared with greater Sydney’s 2.9 per cent. A schooner (425ml) is the default drink size in NSW. “Pints are charged at a premium in NSW and Queensland, compared to the base price of a schooner (425ml),” said Westlake. “In Perth, its more common for a pint to be the base beer price – the fact they are more common could have kept its price down over time.” And in South Australia, a “pint” measures at 425ml, which is a schooner everywhere else; and if you order a schooner in Adelaide, you’ll get a Sydney middy (285ml). Taxed for drinking

Advertisement

Australia has the world’s third-highest alcohol tax rate in the world. One of the biggest factors pushing up beer prices is the twice-yearly alcohol excise increase, which is tied to inflation. Since 2000, beer prices have risen by about 27 per cent after general inflation has been factored in, according to AMP analysis. “In Australia prices have gone up by 113 per cent over the period, but beer prices have gone up a lot more, meaning that’s a real increase in beer prices,” said AMP economist My Bui. “In other words, the nominal increase in beer prices is almost 170 per cent, [so] the real change in beer prices has been about 27 per cent.” Last year, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese made much noise of taking the pressure off beer prices by freezing the excise on draught beer for two years. “[It’s] a commonsense measure that is good for beer drinkers, good for brewers and good for pubs,” he said in March last year. But the temporary freeze is only for the draught (or tap) beer market, 90 per cent of which is controlled by the two foreign Big Alcohol multinationals: Lion, a subsidiary of $21 billion Japanese beverage conglomerate Kirin, and CUB, a subsidiary of Japanese rival Asahi. “All the freeze is doing is giving producers a little breathing room to either not increase prices or to absorb the cost. It will not have any impact on the cost and/or price of beer now,” said Independent Brewers Association chief executive Kylie Lethbridge.

Virgiliu Postolachi has seen up close just how demanding life can be when striving to be recognised among football’s upper echelon after he grew up trying to force his way into one of the world’s most famed powerhouses. The experience tested his resolve and resulted in international stars Edinson Cavani, Presnel Kimpembe and Neymar “pushing him hard” and forcing him to mature quickly during his time growing up within the system of French juggernauts Paris Saint-Germain (PSG). “Sometimes they’d get on me, kick me, but say to me ‘stand up and continue to push’. It was pretty cool,” Postolachi told this masthead. Virgiliu Postolachi has arrived at the Brisbane Roar. “You need to grow up, and you need to listen and take every information fast. You don’t have time, and they don’t let you have mistakes, so you have to keep working and be aware every time.

Advertisement

“OK, they were big players, but I wanted to be better than them. You need to be at the same level when you train with them, so you’re working more hard than them because you’re young.” Related Article Socceroos The curious stat that illustrates Socceroos young gun’s quality Postolachi was just 13 when he arrived at PSG. The Moldovian striker eventually joined fellow French Ligue 1 outfit Lille, where he shared the pitch with Portuguese sensations Jose Fonte and Renato Sanches. But after then taking his talents to Belgium and Romania, the 26-year-old has set his sights on a new challenge: restoring Brisbane Roar to the champion status they enjoyed last decade. Not since the 2020-21 season have the three-time A-League winners featured in the finals race, with the glory days of their trio of titles between the 2010-11 and 2013-14 seasons now a distant memory.

Advertisement

That run of early exits appeared to be on the cusp of ending during their last campaign, before Socceroos defender Lucas Herrington’s transfer to the Colorado Rapids – a move that then inspired his lucrative venture to the Premier League with Hull City. From that point, the Roar would win just once from their remaining 14 clashes. But it was the club’s passionate drive to return to the top that captivated Postolachi and drew him to Australia. “I love the mentality they have in Brisbane. We want this year to do better than last year, to arrive as the top team of Australia, and this motivation is good for me,” he said. Tyrese Francois brings Premier League experience to the Brisbane Roar. “It was a new challenge for me, a new country, new teammates – everything new. I was surprised by the quality of the players we have in the team. Also, the guys have accepted me so fast, and I got used to the training really fast, and adapted really fast.”

Advertisement

In a bid to restore the fallen contenders, coach Michael Valkanis has swept change through his squad. Postolachi is joined by former Fulham midfielder Tyrese Francois, four-time Socceroos defender Joel King, South Korea veteran Nam Tae-hee, and new skipper Tom Aldred as the fresh faces to spearhead Brisbane back to the top. Related Article Socceroos Irankunda senses a dominant decade beckons. Brazil will test that theory “We want to dominate more with the ball this season, that’s no secret. To do that, you need the types of players like Tyrese, like Nam, like Joel being a defender who’s very comfortable with the ball,” Valkanis said. “It’s not just dominating possession for the sake of it, but to be able to create opportunities to score goals. A lot of these players have good mobility and speed, so that’s very important in the A-League, and most of all, they’re the type of characters and people we brought in who will put the team first.” Francois said his “unbelievable” experience growing up in the Fulham system forced him to “grow up really quickly”, given how competitive the sport’s landscape was in England, and how young athletes were thrust into intensive training and competition.

Injuries, however, left him at a crossroads, and despite featuring at Socceroos camps in 2022, he is yet to land on the international stage. But the former Olyroos captain believes he is ready to rediscover his best. “Of course, it’s a dream of mine to play for the Socceroos, but I also understand it’s one step at a time, and the most important step for me right now is to do my best for the Brisbane Roar,” Francois admitted. Loading “I was at a point in my career where I needed a reset. I had some unbelievable experiences abroad, but the last two years have been very difficult for me. I needed a new environment, I needed a new home that would allow me to progress and also do what I know I can do. “Every footballer wants to play, and when you can’t play, you kind of feel useless. You learn very quickly over there that it’s not personal – if you can’t play, you’re not needed in the team.

“I just needed to come back and enjoy my football again – enjoy playing football with a smile on my face and, naturally, my best football will come out.” Postolachi felt the European exposure he and Francois brought would be the tonic needed to arrest Brisbane’s slide and ensure their freefall would not happen again. “We come from Europe, and in Europe there’s relegation, so you fight to keep your place in the first league. On a warm January day in Hawaii in early 1941, a flying boat appeared on the horizon over the sea, and landed in the water outside Honolulu. The plane - a Consolidated PBY Catalina – made its landing on January 27, it had departed from San Diego, where it was built, and it had just accomplished a rare feat. It had spent “almost a full day in the air” traversing 4392km to get to Hawaii. Waiting in Honolulu was a Qantas crew. On July 10, 1943, the first ‘Double Sunrise’ Catalina flight departs Perth for Ceylon (Sri Lanka). This remains the longest scheduled passenger service in the world by elapsed time. Honolulu is where Qantas took its first delivery of the long-range planes that the “Flying Kangaroo” would later enable the Double Sunrise flights - at a distance of 6480 km between Perth and Ceylon, keeping Australia connected with the UK during World War II. Within months of the first plane’s delivery, the Imperial Japanese Navy would stage its infamous surprise attack on US military bases in Hawaii, and the US would declare war on Japan and Germany.

Advertisement

But in early 1941, when the first Catalina plane was to be delivered to Qantas, the US was still neutral, while Australia, with links to the UK, was already at war. The Catalina PBY-6A became the lifeline which helped keep Qantas alive and maintained communications between Australia and the United Kingdom. As a result, the delivery flight “had to be flown by an American crew and that legal title would be transferred to Qantas in Honolulu,” according to academic Silvano Jung. Despite the RAAF pilots being seconded to Qantas, “the aircraft also had to be marked with civilian registration”. Designated VH-AFA, the Australian crew included famed aviator Captain P.G. Taylor. Two days later, the plane left for Canton Island - roughly between Hawaii and Fiji. VH-AFA arrived at Rose Bay, Sydney on February 2, 1941. The delivery flight from Hawaii to Sydney was only the third time the Pacific had been crossed by air. To get from Hawaii to Sydney safely in 1941 required flight crews to use a combination of dead reckoning (calculating location from fixed points), radio direction finding and astronomical navigation, with the Catalina’s blister bubble on top, designed for this purpose.

Advertisement

Japanese forces specifically targeted the PBY Catalinas during the Pearl Harbour attack on December 7, 1941. US Navy photograph But these three methods themselves had to be continually cross-checked to ensure reliability. The Catalina was made for the original Double Sunrise route, connecting Western Australia to Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and onwards to London. The Double Sunrise flights began in 1943, as Japanese forces advanced through South-East Asia, towards Australia. Today, the legacy of those flights lives on in Qantas’ upcoming Project Sunrise project, which is poised to redefine long-haul travel, even as, like in the 1940s, geopolitical uncertainty returns. Right equipment in the right hands Finding the right aircraft for the mission is a recurring theme of the displays at Honolulu’s Pearl Harbour Aviation Museum, home to iconic planes like the B-25 Mitchell and Japanese Mitsubishi A6M “Zero.” The museum recounts Japan’s surprise attack and the Pacific War that followed.

Advertisement

Ultimately, World War II came down to the right equipment in the right hands – and the PBY Catalina was a prime example – in its use by Qantas, but also the RAAF, and the US Navy. The Douglas SBD-2P Dauntless dive bomber, on display at the Pearl Harbor Aviation Museum. It was used in the Battle of the Coral Sea, which relieved the threat to the supply lines between the US and Australia. The Age Beyond civilian transport in Qantas livery, the Catalina military planes played a vital role in patrolling Australia’s vast borders, and they operated across the Pacific as an observation and reconnaissance aircraft. The RAAF ordered 253 of them. As a museum docent, Scott Mensen explained to me, the Catalinas made up patrol fleets in the Pacific during World War II “so they could operate from remote locations because they didn’t need a runway. “Since they could land in the water at any small island they could easily fly to them, and they could fly missions out of those islands.

Advertisement

“They were based all over the Pacific, and they had units that basically took care of the servicing of the aircraft that they could return to.” Recognising their role as the “eyes of the fleet”, the Japanese targeted the Catalinas parked at Pearl Harbour during the attack on December 7 1941. By the time the attack had finished, only 11 of the 61 Catalinas across the island of Oahu were airworthy. One patrol squadron of 12 saw seven of its planes destroyed. US military commanders had grouped them together to guard against potential sabotage by local Japanese spies, which inadvertently made the planes easier targets. A Mitsubishi A6M “Zero” on display at the Pearl Harbour Aviation Museum. The long-range fighter saw action through the Pacific Chris Zappone/The Age Even today in Australia, the legacy of the PBY is evident, as the plane is featured in museums nationwide – from the Qantas founder museum to the Aviation Heritage Museum in Perth. There’s even a monument to the PBY patrols in Cairns.

Advertisement

There is a cluster of Catalina wrecks in Broome that can be visited. A museum in Victoria for the wartime flying boat repair depot in Lake Boga. The hybrid fuselage-hull, dual prop engines mounted over the massive wings and the bulging blister windows out the side are a reminder of how design is shaped by needs. Qantas Catalina flying boat at Karachi in 1945. Alamy Stock Photo In the museum, the individual stories of planes correlate to specific battles. The Battle of Midway turned the tide against the Japanese, the Battle of the Coral Sea relieved the threat to the supply lines between the US and Australia. The museum also highlights how in a crunch, militaries and economies had to scramble to innovate, and – to use a contemporary word – iterate new versions of aircraft. The B-25 Mitchell had to be stripped down and lightened to allow it to conduct the first US bombing raid on Japan, for example. Designers, engineers, and welders worked non-stop to make the changes needed for a mission. Some planes would succeed, while others got consigned to history books (The Brewster F2A Buffalo fighter, anyone?)

Advertisement

Technological progress is rarely a straight line. Radar transformed war in both the Pacific and Europe. Today a Japanese Self-Defence Force member takes a picture of the Ford Island Control Tower. The Age/ Chris Zappone However, in December 1941, radar was a new technology that was not operated continuously. On the morning of December 7, US radar operators detected incoming Japanese aircraft, but officers mistook the signal for a flight of incoming American B-17 bombers from the mainland. The evolving situation of 1941 gives the aviation engineering on display at the museum a poignancy. It also begs the question in our time about what might be the right machines for this era (Ghost Bat? Ghost Shark? Virginia-class subs?)

Advertisement

The correct mix is seemingly one of hardware, lots of software, and humans who can use the technology effectively. Culture, design and war While many aviation museums assemble the odds and ends that are available and put them on display, the Pearl Harbour Aviation Museum boasts a more coherent collection. And the museum had, to me at least, a kind of energy to it, one that can sometimes be absent for aviation museums featuring historical planes. Of course, the Pearl Harbour museum also has the advantage of place. The attack took place on Ford Island. From Ford Island Control Tower, visitors can see with their own eyes the landscape (and airspace) that the Imperial Japanese Navy attacked in 1941. The destroyer USS Shaw explodes after being hit by bombs during the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbour, Hawaii on December 7, 1941. AP

Advertisement

And in fact, the museum sits directly across the water from active base Naval Station Pearl Harbour. Given the sensitive nature of the military bases, visitors without active military ID can only get to the museum by parking at the visitor centre and taking a free bus on to Ford Island. The proximity between history and the present is everywhere. The museum’s CEO is ex-Blue Angel pilot John Hiltz, who, until not so long ago, was flying F/A-18F off aircraft carriers. The museum is nestled in a hive of activity with military planes and ships passing by. Its displays in this setting are a reminder that history, well, it happens sometimes. In 1941, the Americans had based their Pacific fleet in Pearl Harbour on the hunch that Japan would attack further southwest in the Pacific, nearer Australia. The Grumman F4F-3 Wildcat fighter used by the US Marines at Wake Island, the Battle of Coral Sea, and the Battle of Midway. The Age/ Chris Zappone

Advertisement

Instead, a Japanese taskforce set sail in radio silence across a northern route and surprised the US, in an attempt to cripple the entire US fleet. Nearby in the waters surrounding Ford Island lies the USS Arizona Memorial, the resting place for over 1102 service members killed during the surprise assault. Despite its serious, even solemn history, the Pearl Harbour Aviation Museum also celebrates the culture and design and even music of the 1940s - and is friendly to kids and families. The site attracts a wide audience, including families, active-duty military personnel from local bases, and, when I visited, uniformed members of Japan Self-Defence Forces, with rising sun patches on their sleeves, also on site. The ‘Double Sunrise’ Catalinas being serviced on the ramp at Nedlands on the Swan River, with Vega Star in the foreground during WWII. Courage in the Skies (Allen & Unwin, 2017) Australian visitors often take special interest in relics recovered from nearby regions, such as a Nakajima B5N “Kate” torpedo bomber retrieved from Rabaul, Papua New Guinea.

Advertisement

Displayed outside on the tarmac are additional aircraft with Pacific service history, including a Royal Australian Air Force F-111 wearing its full military markings. The museum also owns a Catalina, of course it does, but it is currently being restored in Michigan - before it is returned for public display. Chris Zappone travelled as a guest of Alaska Airlines. title: Battle lines drawn as Curtin opposes WA’s mega-university plan

A leader of one of the state’s major universities says the institution will “vigorously oppose” a planned merger of Curtin, Murdoch and the University of WA after the Cook government announced it will progress a business case to create a mega-university. Curtin University vice-chancellor Harlene Hayne. Premier Roger Cook and Tertiary and International Education Minister Tony Buti on Sunday announced plans to build a business case to guide the proposed merge of three of the state’s top universities before a final decision is made. According to the state government, the plan will be undertaken by the Department of the Premier and Cabinet, with input from a steering committee led by Western Australian businessman Mark Barnaba as chair and medical researcher Professor Fiona Wood as deputy chair. However, Curtin University vice chancellor Professor Harlene Hayne expressed deep concern about the merger and said the institution is planning to oppose the proposal.

Advertisement

“Curtin will vigorously oppose this in the best interests of our more than 67,000 students, 10,000 staff, 300,000 graduates and Western Australia’s economic future,” she said. “Cost, waste, and loss of choice, jobs and legacy will be the hallmarks of the planned merger of universities proposed by the Western Australian government today. “Every graduate of UWA, Curtin and Murdoch holds a degree from an institution that may not exist in the future.” Hayne said while the benefits of a potential merger have never been clearly articulated by the state government, she is also aware of the significant costs, risks and disruptions a merger would create for WA’s future. “We have been clear from the outset that Curtin does not support a forced merger,” she said.

Advertisement

“A three-way merger of Curtin, UWA and Murdoch would create a mega-university of almost 120,000 students - a scale unmatched in Australia and rare internationally. Size at that level brings complexity, not competitiveness, and draws efforts away from our core purposes of teaching, learning and student support. Related Article Exclusive

University Are WA’s universities ‘scaremongering’ over merger plans? “As WA faces a cost-of-living crisis, housing pressures, critical shortages of healthcare workers and growing pressure on hospital beds, I can’t see how spending more than a billion dollars in this way will benefit Western Australians.” Then-education minister Tony Buti commissioned a review of the state’s tertiary sector in 2023 after concerns were raised about plummeting student numbers and research grants, and WA university standings compared to their east coast counterparts. The review prompted Buti to commission a cost-benefit analysis of the three merger options mid- last year, which was led by former Labor heavyweight Alannah MacTiernan.

Advertisement

According to the state government, both studies found that merging the three WA public universities would provide maximum benefits to the WA economy and the creation of long-term jobs for Western Australians. They also found that WA is missing out on vital international and national research funding, which a strengthened university will be better positioned to win, further boosting the WA economy. Buti said the business case is a critical step towards determining the best approach to maintaining a modern, globally competitive university sector here in Western Australia for the long-term. “We have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to secure the future education of our children and future leaders and strengthen our economy by ensuring our higher education offerings remain relevant and attractive, so it is important we get this right,” he said. “Western Australia not only needs to deliver world-class education for students; we also need to build on our existing capability to deliver leading research.

Advertisement

“The business case is about doing the detailed work - confirming costs, transition arrangements, and implementation pathways ahead of a final decision being made.” Cook said ensuring local workers have the skills needed for WA’s jobs of the future is one of his government’s top priorities. “We have rebuilt our TAFE campuses and made hundreds of priority courses free for Western Australians, so we can get more local workers into local jobs,” he said. “The next opportunity to get WA workers job-ready is to ensure that we have a world-class university system that is delivering for Western Australians right across our State. “While the reports we have undertaken to date have identified the benefits of university mergers, we need to do more work on the potential costs and ability for the reforms to be funded by the universities themselves before making a final decision.”

Advertisement

WA opposition education spokesman Liam Staltari raised concerns over the cost of the proposal to the state’s taxpayers. “I think the jobs it will create are for the lawyers and consultants who will pick over a merger process for years at a time, which is exactly the concern that we have, and which would not deliver value for money for taxpayers,” he said. “We haven’t seen the review, we haven’t seen the cost-benefit analysis, and if the cost-benefit analysis doesn’t capture the cost, then actually it’s not worth the paper it’s written on.”

Hamming it up in front of more than 5000 devoted Samoa fans at Mt Druitt on Saturday, Jarome Luai was in his element. Tossing his cap into the crowd after excitedly joining his international teammates on stage, the 29-year-old was given a rapturous reception. Jarome Luai (centre) and Junior Paulo (right) will play together for Parramatta as well as Samoa. NRL Wests Tigers supporters probably don’t feel as warmly about him after his much-discussed mid-contract signing with the PNG Chiefs and eventual exit. But Luai’s new club teammate and national captain Junior Paulo has welcomed the five-eighth with open arms to Parramatta, where he will spend next season before heading to Port Moresby.

Advertisement

There is a Samoan infusion coming at the Eels, with Spencer Leniu, Jaydn Su’A and Luai joining seasoned front-rower Paulo and Ronald Volkman at their Kellyville base. Luai will only be there for a year, as Jonah Pezet was last season before linking with the Broncos, but Parramatta plan to make the most of it. Jarome Luai’s time at the Tigers did not pan out as planned. Sydney Morning Herald, Getty, NRL Images Speaking at the launch of the World Cup in Sydney, Paulo threw his support behind the four-time grand final winner, who drew headlines for flying to PNG for sponsorship appearances while at the Tigers and for missing the club’s presentation night last month. “As someone who knows him … he’s someone that is misunderstood. He’s a competitor, and I think it’s probably been a bit unfair, the treatment that he’s copped over recent weeks,” he said.

Advertisement

“He hasn’t done any wrong. It’s just one of those things where there’s always going to be someone who’s opinionated. Luckily for ‘Rome’, nothing fazes him. “There’s a reason why he’s won four comps, so that’s the experience we want to bring at Parramatta. We’re looking forward to it.” Jarome Luai at the Samoa fan day on Saturday. Instagram The addition of Leniu on a four-year deal is another plus for Parramatta coach Jason Ryles. The former Penrith forward is returning to Sydney’s west after winning a fourth premiership ring with the Roosters last Sunday. Leniu’s devastating cameo off the bench against Newcastle helped turn the match in favour of the Roosters.

Advertisement

“When you look at those guys’ resumes, there’s a lot of experience that you’re bringing into the team. Those guys know how to win,” said Paulo, who is close to agreeing to an extension with the Eels himself following a contract standoff. “Spencer has always been a firecracker … when you do it the way he did it [in the grand final] it was momentum changing for the Roosters. Luckily for us at Parra, now we get to have him on our side.” Spencer Leniu shows off his premiership ring after the grand final. Getty Images Before then, the Eels’ Samoa contingent have their eyes on the World Cup. Finalists against Australia at Old Trafford in the 2022 edition of the tournament, the quality of their squad indicates they can again contend for the cup.

Advertisement

Aside from Luai, Leniu and Paulo, the Samoa squad features superstars such as Stephen Crichton, Brian To’o and Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow as well as electric Melbourne fullback Sua Fa’alogo and emerging talents such as Jermaine McEwen and Francis Manuleleua, who excelled in the Knights’ run to the grand final. Related Article Rugby League World Cup ‘Fingers crossed’: Walker hopes to secure new Roosters deal before November 1 Samoa begin their campaign with a group-stage game against France at CommBank Stadium on Friday night and are looking to make more history after their landmark appearance in the final four years ago. “We addressed it early when we got into camp that we don’t want to be the team that sort of dwells on those memories, although they were very good ones,” said Paulo. “We want to be able to build and move forward and hit the ground running in this World Cup. We want to be able to make a statement.”

The Wallabies were taken to the hurt locker by the All Blacks on Saturday, and the methodology used against them would have been all-too-familiar. Former Wallabies coach Dave Rennie’s imprint was all over the All Blacks’ performance, so the Wallabies knew what was coming and will feel a little disappointed at how they failed to stop it. The high ball was an issue, but it’s an issue for everyone these days, and the Wallabies’ main area of improvement before the rematch in Sydney on Saturday will be to put some pressure on the ball carrier. Loading Even in the first half, players such as All Blacks No.8 Wallace Sititi were happily taking the space offered to him by the Wallabies. The All Blacks had two or three metres to wind up before they hit the advantage line and it was a factor that took a massive toll as the Test wore on. Some Wallabies jackallers will feel they didn’t get much protection from the officials when the All Blacks came in from the side, but if you can’t stop a Rennie side on the gainline they are going to keep coming to unleash a back line that has markedly improved since last year.

Advertisement

The good news for the Wallabies is that they can resolve the issue, but they’ll need to get in the faces of the All Blacks on Saturday. Suaalii’s tackle technique remains an issue Joseph Aukuso-Suaalii can’t seem to get some bad habits out of his game. His no-arms tackle on Jordie Barrett in the 69th minute was no doubt borne out of frustration, but he is developing a reputation as a dangerous tackler. It’s a shame because Suaalii’s shift to the wing is unlocking his athletic potential on attack. However, his tackle on Barrett wasn’t even close to being legal and his defensive reads will be targeted by the All Blacks. All Blacks halfback Cam Roigard puts boot to ball against the Wallabies. Getty Images Hip-drop blitz is coming to rugby

Advertisement

Rob Valetini’s tackle on Leroy Carter in the second half at Eden Park will be illegal from November 1 – and will likely result in a ban. Carter was injured in Valetini’s hip-drop tackle and there is no doubt that it can cause damage, but players will be in a race against time to change their techniques for the end-of-year tour. World Rugby issued the update on the hip-drop tackle earlier this week, and said they were relatively rare, but once you start looking for illegalities in rugby you’ll tend to find them. Smaller players, such as No.9s and No.10s, are particularly prone to using the hip-drop tackles as a way of bringing bigger opponents to the ground, so the November Tests may open up a can of worms. Related Article Australian rugby Ikitau out of Sydney Bledisloe but Valetini to avoid hip-drop scrutiny Why the high ball is so hard to defend There was a moment in the second half that summed up the Wallabies’ struggles under the high ball – All Blacks halfback Cam Roigard put up a box kick from inside his own territory and No.6 Tupou Vaa’i ran on to the ball at full speed to regather it. After escort runners were deemed to be illegal at the end of 2024, the team kicking the ball has all the rights in the high-ball contest. A few years ago, there is no way the Wallabies would have let Vaa’i run a clear line to get that box kick: he would have been shepherded out of the way. As noted in the top item, the high ball is a headache for everyone in Test rugby: even the Springboks struggled with it against the Wallabies in Perth. The rewards are coming for teams who kick well, and Wallabies halfback Ryan Lonergan was second best to Roigard on Saturday. It was uncharacteristic from Lonergan, but he was one of many Wallabies who had an off night in Auckland. Paradoxically, his sub-par performance reflected how important he has become for Les Kiss’ side. Dan Botha on the charge for the Waratahs. Getty Images

Advertisement

The Tahs prop involved in a scrum clinic It’s a long way from Sydney to Whangarei in New Zealand’s far north in more ways than one, but Waratahs prop Dan Botha looks as happy as a pig in muck. Botha played a key role in Northland’s quarter-final win against Tasman in New Zealand’s NPC on Friday, anchoring his team’s dominant scrum. Northland have used that set-piece as a weapon all season, winning penalty after penalty, so it is highly likely that Botha will return to Australia with a few new tricks up his sleeve. The Waratahs will be delighted, because Botha will now get to play in a semi-final and experience all the pressure that goes with that. The prop wasn’t first choice for a lot of the Northland campaign, but injury gave him an opportunity and he has grabbed it with both hands. He even performed in a stirring team haka before the quarter-final, so the move to New Zealand has been a rich experience for the 24-year-old.

title: Twin brothers win Lotto twice in two years
text:
Twin brothers have defied the odds and are planning to hit the road after they celebrated their second lotto win within two years.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

The first win helped them buy their sister's home, now they can pay off the property and hit the road.

Both winning tickets were purchased from Clark's Newsagency in Albany.

The Albany brothers, 65, from Western Australia's Great Southern, shared a $1m Millionaire Medley prize within two years of winning Set For Life.

One of the lucky brothers said he bought the ticket after his dentist appointment was cancelled.

"When I got home, I realised I'd bought a Slikpik and forgotten to get my usual numbers as well," he said.

"I wouldn't usually ever buy more than one ticket a day, but when I realised I'd only bought the Slikpik, I thought I'd pop back because I like playing the same numbers.

"I know it's completely random, but it's what I like to do."

The second trip to the retailer resulted in a System 8 entry that secured the $1 million prize.

"We're set now," one brother said.

"We've worked physically demanding jobs our whole lives but now we can relax a bit more, pay the house off and then we both want to get caravans so we can travel around Australia together."

The twin brothers have won Lotto twice within two years.

While one brother is dreaming of life on the road, the other has already celebrated in his own way.

"I bought myself a watch because you have to treat yourself a bit," he said.

"I also like disco and dancing, so I might celebrate with my girlfriend."

Lotterywest spokesman Nikki Wilson-Smith said it was rare to welcome the same players back to the Winners Room for a second major prize.

"Winning a major prize is a memorable moment for any player, but to experience two significant wins within such a short period is remarkable," she said.

"It's wonderful to see these brothers using their prizes to secure their future and enjoy retirement together."
